title: Entity identity versus record identity
description: A practical guide to separating a business entity from the records that observe it, using a hypothetical retail customer dataset with counterexamples and diagnostics.
lead: A row is not always the thing your business is talking about. In customer, product, account, and order models, one business entity can be observed by many records, and one careless identifier can either split that entity apart or merge it with something else. The practical modeling task is to make entity identity and record identity separate, explicit, and testable.

sections.heading: The distinction
paragraphs: Record identity answers this question: which stored observation are we talking about? Entity identity answers a different question: which business thing is this observation about?

A source customer row, a point-of-sale receipt, a support ticket, and a web profile can all describe the same customer. Each record needs its own identity because each record has its own provenance, timestamp, payload, and correction history. The customer also needs an identity, but that identity is not automatically the same as any one record key from any one system.

This matters because relational design depends on choosing the key that determines the facts in a table. A record key can determine the attributes captured on that record: source system, source record key, observed email, observed phone number, observed order total, and observed time. A business entity key should identify the real-world or business-defined thing being tracked across those records. If the two ideas are collapsed, the model starts making false promises. It may imply that an email address uniquely determines a customer, that a source record is the customer, or that the latest row overwrites the truth of earlier observations.

This article assumes you already know what candidate keys and alternate keys are. The problem here is not merely selecting one key from a list. The problem is recognizing when the candidate key belongs to the record grain rather than the entity grain.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail example with counterexamples
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retailer with three systems: an ecommerce site, a point-of-sale system, and a support platform. The retailer wants a customer model for analytics. The raw observations below are intentionally small but include common identity traps.

The raw rows are observations, not customers: record 1 is an ecommerce profile for source customer W17 with email lena@example.com, phone 555-0101, loyalty card L88, observed on 2026-02-01. Record 2 is a store receipt for POS customer P9 with no email, phone 555-0101, loyalty card L88, observed on 2026-02-03. Record 3 is a support contact S44 with email lena.returns@example.com, phone 555-0101, no loyalty card, observed on 2026-02-04. Record 4 is an ecommerce profile W22 with email marco@example.com, phone 555-0101, loyalty card L91, observed on 2026-02-05. Record 5 is a support contact S45 with email lena@example.com, phone 555-0199, loyalty card L88, observed on 2026-02-08.

Several tempting shortcuts fail. If email is treated as the customer identity, records 1 and 5 appear to be the same customer, record 3 becomes a different customer, and record 2 may be left unmatched. That may be wrong if Lena used a returns-specific email address with support. If phone is treated as the customer identity, records 1, 2, 3, and 4 all collapse into one customer because the phone number is shared. That may be a household phone, a recycled number, or an entry error. If the source customer ID is treated as the customer identity, W17, P9, S44, W22, and S45 are all separate, even where loyalty card L88 strongly suggests that some observations belong together. If the latest row is treated as the customer, earlier evidence is overwritten and the model loses the ability to explain why a match was made.

The safer interpretation is that each raw row has record identity. The business entity is inferred or assigned separately. For this hypothetical example, a reviewer might decide that records 1, 2, 3, and 5 refer to customer entity C100 because loyalty card L88 and the surrounding attributes support that conclusion, while record 4 refers to customer entity C200 because loyalty card L91 and the different email indicate a different customer despite the shared phone number.

The important point is not that this matching decision is universally correct. It is that the model has a place to store the distinction. The records remain records. The entity assignment is represented as a relationship that can be audited, revised, and governed.
bullets: Counterexample 1: One entity, many records. C100 is observed by web, POS, and support records.
Counterexample 2: One weak identifier, many possible entities. Phone 555-0101 appears on both C100 and C200 observations.
Counterexample 3: One entity, changing attributes. C100 has more than one observed email and phone over time.
Counterexample 4: One source key, limited scope. W17 is meaningful inside the web system, not across every business system.

codeExamples.code:
-- Hypothetical fixture for discussion; not a claim of executed production code.
with raw_customer_observation as (
  select * from (values
    (1, 'web',     'W17', timestamp '2026-02-01 09:00:00', 'lena@example.com',         '555-0101', 'L88'),
    (2, 'pos',     'P9',  timestamp '2026-02-03 14:20:00', null,                       '555-0101', 'L88'),
    (3, 'support', 'S44', timestamp '2026-02-04 11:10:00', 'lena.returns@example.com', '555-0101', null),
    (4, 'web',     'W22', timestamp '2026-02-05 16:45:00', 'marco@example.com',        '555-0101', 'L91'),
    (5, 'support', 'S45', timestamp '2026-02-08 08:30:00', 'lena@example.com',         '555-0199', 'L88')
  ) as t(record_id, source_system, source_customer_id, observed_at, email, phone, loyalty_card)
)
select *
from raw_customer_observation
order by record_id;

sections.heading: Model the two identities explicitly
paragraphs: A durable pattern is to separate observations, entities, identifiers, and the links between them. The observation table is at the record grain. It preserves what a source said at a time. The entity table is at the business entity grain. It represents the customer, supplier, account, device, or product that the business wants to reason about across systems. The link table records the assertion that a given observation is about a given entity, along with the matching rule or stewardship decision that produced the assertion.

This structure avoids pretending that every attribute belongs on the entity row. A current preferred email might be useful, but it is not the same thing as every observed email. The observation row can say what was captured. A derived current profile can say which value is currently preferred. The entity row itself should be kept narrow unless the attribute truly belongs to the entity grain.

Identifier tables are also useful because identifiers have scope. A source customer ID is scoped to its source system. A loyalty card number may be scoped to a loyalty program. An email address may be an observed contact method, not a permanent identity. Modeling that scope keeps the design honest.
A simplified relational shape is shown below. It is not a complete customer data platform design. It is a minimal structure for preserving the difference between record identity and entity identity.
bullets: customer_entity contains one row per business entity the organization chooses to track.
customer_observation contains one row per observed source record or event at its original record grain.
customer_entity_observation links observations to entities and stores the basis for the assignment.
customer_identifier stores scoped identifiers associated with an entity, ideally with source, type, and validity metadata where the business needs it.

codeExamples.code:
-- Simplified logical schema for the pattern.
create table customer_entity (
  customer_entity_id varchar(20) primary key,
  created_reason varchar(100) not null
);

create table customer_observation (
  record_id integer primary key,
  source_system varchar(30) not null,
  source_customer_id varchar(50) not null,
  observed_at timestamp not null,
  observed_email varchar(320),
  observed_phone varchar(40),
  observed_loyalty_card varchar(50),
  unique (source_system, source_customer_id, observed_at)
);

create table customer_entity_observation (
  customer_entity_id varchar(20) not null references customer_entity(customer_entity_id),
  record_id integer not null references customer_observation(record_id),
  match_rule_id varchar(50) not null,
  assignment_status varchar(20) not null,
  primary key (customer_entity_id, record_id)
);

create table customer_identifier (
  customer_entity_id varchar(20) not null references customer_entity(customer_entity_id),
  identifier_type varchar(30) not null,
  identifier_value varchar(320) not null,
  identifier_scope varchar(50) not null,
  first_observed_at timestamp not null,
  primary key (identifier_type, identifier_value, identifier_scope, customer_entity_id)
);

sections.heading: Ask what depends on what
paragraphs: The modeling diagnostic is simple: ask which key determines the fact you are storing. If the fact is what one source record said at one time, it depends on the record identity. If the fact is an assignment made by an identity process, it depends on the pair of entity identity and record identity. If the fact is a scoped identifier associated with an entity, it depends on the entity plus the identifier type, value, and scope. If the fact is a business-wide customer attribute, make sure the organization can define when that attribute is true and how conflicting observations are resolved.

For the hypothetical data, record_id 1 determines that the web system observed lena@example.com and phone 555-0101 on 2026-02-01. Customer entity C100 does not determine a single observed email, because C100 has multiple observations. Phone 555-0101 does not determine a single customer entity, because it appears on observations assigned to both C100 and C200. Loyalty card L88 may be a stronger identifier in this dataset, but the model should still record its scope and the rule that used it.

This is where normalization vocabulary is helpful without turning the article into a full normalization lesson. Functional dependency thinking asks whether one set of attributes determines another. When a table mixes entity-grain facts and record-grain facts, apparent dependencies become ambiguous. The cure is not to make the model more abstract; it is to put each fact at the grain where it is actually true.
bullets: Record-grain fact: record 5 observed phone 555-0199.
Entity-grain assertion: record 5 is assigned to customer entity C100.
Identifier-grain fact: loyalty card L88 is associated with C100 within the retailer loyalty program.
Derived profile fact: C100 currently prefers a selected contact email, according to a documented survivorship rule.

sections.heading: Diagnostics for existing tables
paragraphs: Existing warehouse tables often reveal this confusion through duplicate counts and contradictory attributes. The following diagnostics are not a complete data quality suite, but they help locate places where record identity has been mistaken for entity identity or where weak identifiers are being used as if they were unique.

The first diagnostic looks for a supposed entity key that appears to be only a source record key. If every entity has exactly one observation, the model may simply have renamed records as entities. That can be valid for some domains, but it is suspicious when the business expects cross-system identity resolution.

The second diagnostic looks for identifiers that map to multiple entities. This is not automatically an error. A household phone, shared business email, recycled device ID, or data entry mistake can all produce this result. The point is to prevent the model from silently treating such identifiers as globally unique when the data does not support that assumption.

The third diagnostic looks for entities with multiple current-looking values for attributes that downstream users may assume are single valued. That finding should trigger a design question: should the table store all observations, a current selected value, or both?

codeExamples.code:
-- Diagnostic 1: entities with only one linked observation.
-- Useful when the domain should contain entities observed across multiple records.
select
  customer_entity_id,
  count(*) as linked_observation_count
from customer_entity_observation
where assignment_status = 'active'
group by customer_entity_id
having count(*) = 1;

-- Diagnostic 2: identifier values linked to more than one entity in the same scope.
select
  identifier_type,
  identifier_value,
  identifier_scope,
  count(distinct customer_entity_id) as entity_count
from customer_identifier
group by identifier_type, identifier_value, identifier_scope
having count(distinct customer_entity_id) > 1;

-- Diagnostic 3: entities with more than one observed email across linked records.
select
  ceo.customer_entity_id,
  count(distinct co.observed_email) as observed_email_count
from customer_entity_observation ceo
join customer_observation co
  on co.record_id = ceo.record_id
where co.observed_email is not null
  and ceo.assignment_status = 'active'
group by ceo.customer_entity_id
having count(distinct co.observed_email) > 1;

sections.heading: Tradeoffs and boundaries
paragraphs: Separating entity identity from record identity adds tables and requires stewardship rules. That cost is worthwhile when the business needs to reconcile multiple systems, preserve history, audit matching decisions, or revise identity assignments. It may be unnecessary for a small table where each row truly is the business entity and there are no separate observations to preserve.

The main tradeoff is that the entity key becomes an assertion, not a raw fact. Someone or something assigns observations to an entity. The assignment might come from deterministic rules, human review, probabilistic matching, or a vendor system. The model should store enough metadata to explain the assignment at the level the organization needs. It should not pretend that the assignment is the same kind of fact as a source record timestamp.

Another boundary is metric grain. Order quantities, sales amounts, support interactions, and inventory movements often belong to event or fact records, not to the entity row. Dimensional modeling guidance commonly emphasizes being explicit about measurement grain and units. The same habit applies here: do not move facts to the entity table just because the entity is important.

A useful final test is to read a table name and its key aloud. If the table is called customer but the key is source_system plus source_customer_id, it may be a source customer record table, not a customer entity table. If the table is called customer_profile but contains many observed emails and phones over time, it may be an observation history. Clear naming will not solve identity resolution, but it will make incorrect assumptions easier to see.

takeaways: A record key identifies an observation; an entity key identifies the business thing that observations are about.
Do not treat email, phone, source customer ID, or latest row as a universal entity identity without checking scope and counterexamples.
Model observations, entities, identifiers, and entity-observation assignments separately when the business needs cross-record identity.
Ask what each fact depends on: the record, the entity, the identifier scope, or a derived survivorship rule.
Diagnostics for one-to-one entity-record patterns, identifiers shared across entities, and conflicting observed attributes can reveal identity modeling mistakes.

title: Optional relationships in data models
description: A practical guide to modeling absent relationships directly, using nullable foreign keys, relationship tables, and explicit reason attributes instead of fabricated default entities.
lead: Optional relationships are common: an order may not have a sales representative, a customer may not have a referrer, and a shipment may not have a return authorization. The modeling mistake is to hide that absence behind fabricated rows such as Unknown Customer, No Campaign, or Unassigned Rep. Those rows look convenient at first, but they turn absence into a fake entity and make downstream logic harder to trust. A better model represents the missing relationship as missing, while preserving the ability to explain why it is missing when that explanation matters.

sections.heading: The problem with default entities
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail-order system. Each order may be associated with a registered customer, a marketing campaign, and a store associate. Some orders are guest checkouts. Some orders are not campaign-driven. Some online orders have no associate. These are normal business facts, not data quality failures by themselves.

A common shortcut is to create default dimension rows: customer_id = 0 for Unknown Customer, campaign_id = 0 for No Campaign, and associate_id = 0 for Unassigned Associate. This makes every foreign key non-null. It can also make joins look simpler because every order appears to have a customer, campaign, and associate. The cost is semantic damage: the model now says a relationship exists when the business fact is that it does not.

The shortcut creates several problems. Counts become ambiguous because Unknown Customer is not a customer, No Campaign is not a campaign, and Unassigned Associate is not an associate. Data quality checks become weaker because a required relationship and an optional relationship both look populated. Analysts must remember to exclude special rows from metrics. Worse, those exclusions differ by metric: an order with no customer may still count toward revenue, but it should not count as a known-customer purchase.

Relational modeling gives you better tools. A foreign key can represent a relationship to an existing row. A nullable foreign key can represent an optional relationship where the relationship may be absent. A separate relationship table can represent optional many-to-many relationships. A reason attribute can explain absence without pretending that absence is an entity.

sections.heading: Model absence as absence
paragraphs: A cleaner design starts by naming the relationship and deciding whether it is optional. If an order may be placed by a registered customer, then customer_id on the order can be nullable. If it is present, the foreign key must refer to a real customer. If it is absent, the column is null. The null does not mean the customer row exists but is unknown; it means there is no customer relationship recorded for this order.

This distinction matters. A nullable foreign key separates two statements: the relationship is not mandatory, and when the relationship is present it must be valid. Database constraint documentation commonly describes foreign keys as constraints that values in one table must match values in another table. In SQL databases, nullable foreign key columns are often used for optional relationships because no referenced row is required when the referencing value is null. The exact enforcement details should be checked in the target database, but the modeling idea is durable: absence is not a special parent row.

Here is a compact hypothetical schema. It keeps real entities in their own tables and lets optional relationships be null on the order record. It also adds reason columns where the reason for absence is useful to the business.

The reason columns are deliberately not foreign keys to fake entities. For example, customer_absence_reason describes why customer_id is null. It does not claim that a synthetic customer placed the order. A check constraint can keep the relationship and its reason aligned: if customer_id is present, the absence reason should be null; if customer_id is absent, the reason should be populated when the business requires an explanation.

codeExamples.code:
-- Hypothetical retail model: optional relationships are represented directly.
create table customer (
  customer_id integer primary key,
  customer_number text not null unique,
  customer_name text not null
);

create table campaign (
  campaign_id integer primary key,
  campaign_code text not null unique,
  campaign_name text not null
);

create table associate (
  associate_id integer primary key,
  associate_number text not null unique,
  associate_name text not null
);

create table retail_order (
  order_id integer primary key,
  order_number text not null unique,
  order_total numeric(12,2) not null,

  -- Optional relationship: guest checkout orders have no registered customer.
  customer_id integer null references customer(customer_id),
  customer_absence_reason text null,

  -- Optional relationship: not every order comes from a campaign.
  campaign_id integer null references campaign(campaign_id),
  campaign_absence_reason text null,

  -- Optional relationship: self-service online orders have no associate.
  associate_id integer null references associate(associate_id),
  associate_absence_reason text null,

  check (
    (customer_id is not null and customer_absence_reason is null)
    or
    (customer_id is null and customer_absence_reason in ('guest_checkout', 'not_captured'))
  ),
  check (
    (campaign_id is not null and campaign_absence_reason is null)
    or
    (campaign_id is null and campaign_absence_reason in ('organic', 'not_attributed'))
  ),
  check (
    (associate_id is not null and associate_absence_reason is null)
    or
    (associate_id is null and associate_absence_reason in ('online_self_service', 'not_assigned'))
  )
);

sections.heading: Worked example with real and absent relationships
paragraphs: Populate the hypothetical model with a few rows. The important part is not the retail domain; it is the contrast between real relationships and absent relationships.

Order R-1001 is a guest checkout with no campaign and no associate. Order R-1002 is a known customer order attributed to a campaign but with no associate because it was online self-service. Order R-1003 is a known customer order handled by an associate but not attributed to a campaign. The model can state each fact without inventing Customer 0, Campaign 0, or Associate 0.

This lets downstream queries be honest. If a metric needs only revenue, all orders count. If a metric needs known-customer revenue, only orders with customer_id present count. If a metric needs unaffiliated campaign revenue, it can filter for campaign_id is null and examine campaign_absence_reason. The absence is queryable without being disguised as a dimension member.

The result set from the example query would have three different relationship states. R-1001 has no customer_name, no campaign_name, and no associate_name. R-1002 has a customer and campaign, but no associate. R-1003 has a customer and associate, but no campaign. The outer joins preserve the orders while showing which optional relationships are absent.

codeExamples.code:
insert into customer (customer_id, customer_number, customer_name) values
  (1, 'C-001', 'Asha Rao'),
  (2, 'C-002', 'Miguel Santos');

insert into campaign (campaign_id, campaign_code, campaign_name) values
  (10, 'WELCOME10', 'Welcome discount');

insert into associate (associate_id, associate_number, associate_name) values
  (20, 'A-020', 'Nora Kim');

insert into retail_order
  (order_id, order_number, order_total,
   customer_id, customer_absence_reason,
   campaign_id, campaign_absence_reason,
   associate_id, associate_absence_reason)
values
  (1001, 'R-1001', 42.50,
   null, 'guest_checkout',
   null, 'organic',
   null, 'online_self_service'),

  (1002, 'R-1002', 88.00,
   1, null,
   10, null,
   null, 'online_self_service'),

  (1003, 'R-1003', 19.95,
   2, null,
   null, 'organic',
   20, null);

select
  o.order_number,
  o.order_total,
  c.customer_name,
  o.customer_absence_reason,
  m.campaign_name,
  o.campaign_absence_reason,
  a.associate_name,
  o.associate_absence_reason
from retail_order o
left join customer c on c.customer_id = o.customer_id
left join campaign m on m.campaign_id = o.campaign_id
left join associate a on a.associate_id = o.associate_id
order by o.order_number;

sections.heading: When a null foreign key is not enough
paragraphs: Nullable foreign keys work well for optional one-to-one or many-to-one relationships: an order may have zero or one customer; an order may have zero or one campaign; an order may have zero or one associate. They are not the right shape for every optional relationship.

If an order may be connected to many promotions, do not add promotion_id_1, promotion_id_2, and promotion_id_3 columns. Also do not create a No Promotion row and attach it to every order without a promotion. Use a relationship table. The absence of rows in the relationship table means the order has no promotions. When rows exist, each row must point to a real order and a real promotion.

This is a subtle but important point: absence can live in different places depending on the relationship shape. For a single optional parent, absence can be null in the foreign key column. For an optional collection, absence is usually zero rows in the relationship table. Both patterns avoid fabricated default entities.

If the business needs to distinguish no promotions eligible from promotions not captured, add an attribute to the order or to an assessment table that records the classification. Do not overload a fake promotion row to carry that meaning. A promotion is a promotion; an assessment of why no promotion applies is a different fact.

codeExamples.code:
create table promotion (
  promotion_id integer primary key,
  promotion_code text not null unique,
  promotion_name text not null
);

create table order_promotion (
  order_id integer not null references retail_order(order_id),
  promotion_id integer not null references promotion(promotion_id),
  primary key (order_id, promotion_id)
);

-- No rows in order_promotion for order 1001 means:
-- order 1001 has no promotion relationship recorded.

insert into promotion (promotion_id, promotion_code, promotion_name) values
  (30, 'FREESHIP', 'Free shipping offer'),
  (31, 'BUNDLE5', 'Bundle discount');

insert into order_promotion (order_id, promotion_id) values
  (1002, 30),
  (1002, 31);

select
  o.order_number,
  count(op.promotion_id) as promotion_count
from retail_order o
left join order_promotion op on op.order_id = o.order_id
group by o.order_number
order by o.order_number;

sections.heading: Diagnose and repair a fabricated default
paragraphs: The easiest diagnostic is to search for dimension rows whose business identity is actually an absence label. Names such as Unknown, N/A, None, Unassigned, Not Applicable, No Campaign, and Guest Customer are warning signs. They are not always wrong; a source system may send such codes, and a staging model may need to preserve them. But in an analytical or relational model that is meant to describe business entities, these rows should be challenged.

Ask four questions. First, is this row a real entity with its own identity, lifecycle, and attributes? Second, does relating a fact to this row make a true statement? Third, would users need to exclude this row from entity counts? Fourth, is the model using this row to avoid nullable foreign keys or zero-row relationship tables? If the answers are no, no, yes, and yes, the row is probably a fabricated default entity.

A safe repair is usually incremental. Add nullable relationship columns or relationship tables in the target model. Convert references to fabricated default rows into null relationship values. Preserve the reason separately if it is meaningful. Add constraints that prevent contradictory states, such as a present customer_id with customer_absence_reason = guest_checkout. Update downstream queries so they use is null, is not null, and reason attributes rather than special dimension keys.

There is one tradeoff to acknowledge. Nullable relationships require query authors to understand outer joins and null-aware filters. Fabricated default rows can feel simpler because inner joins keep every fact row. But that simplicity is purchased by lying about the relationship. For a data model intended to support reliable analytics, it is better to make absence explicit and teach the correct query pattern.
bullets: Use a nullable foreign key when a fact can have zero or one related entity.
Use a relationship table when a fact can have zero, one, or many related entities.
Use a reason attribute or classification table when the business cares why the relationship is absent.
Avoid fabricated default rows unless the row represents a real business entity, not merely a missing relationship.

codeExamples.code:
-- Repair pattern for a model that used customer_id = 0 as Unknown Customer.
-- This example assumes retail_order_bad has already been loaded.

create table retail_order_repaired as
select
  order_id,
  order_number,
  order_total,
  case when customer_id = 0 then null else customer_id end as customer_id,
  case when customer_id = 0 then 'guest_or_unknown' else null end as customer_absence_reason,
  case when campaign_id = 0 then null else campaign_id end as campaign_id,
  case when campaign_id = 0 then 'not_attributed' else null end as campaign_absence_reason,
  case when associate_id = 0 then null else associate_id end as associate_id,
  case when associate_id = 0 then 'not_assigned' else null end as associate_absence_reason
from retail_order_bad;

-- In a production migration, constraints would be added deliberately after validation.
-- The key modeling move is: default entity references become absent relationships,
-- and explanations become attributes rather than fake parent rows.

takeaways: Do not model absence by creating fake entities such as Unknown Customer or No Campaign. They make nonexistent relationships look real.
For optional zero-or-one relationships, use nullable foreign keys with constraints that validate real references when values are present.
For optional collections, use a relationship table; zero related rows is a valid way to represent no relationship.
If the reason for absence matters, store the reason as a separate attribute or classification, not as a fabricated dimension member.

title: Cardinality and participation constraints
description: A practical guide to specifying relationship multiplicity and mandatory participation in a relational model, using a hypothetical retail dataset with counterexamples and diagnostic SQL.
lead: Cardinality and participation constraints answer two different questions that are often collapsed into one drawing. Cardinality says how many related rows are allowed. Participation says whether a related row is required. A useful relational model states both.

sections.heading: Two questions, not one
paragraphs: When practitioners say a customer has many orders, they are usually talking about maximum cardinality: more than one order may reference the same customer. That statement is incomplete. It does not say whether every order must have a customer, whether every customer must have at least one order, or whether an order may exist before its lines are loaded.

A relationship specification should answer both the maximum and the minimum question on each side. Maximum cardinality gives the familiar one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many patterns. Minimum participation gives the required or optional part: zero allowed, or at least one required.

A compact way to write this is min..max beside each entity in the relationship. For example, Customer 0..* to Order 1..1 means a customer may have zero or many orders, while each order must reference exactly one customer. The first side is optional participation with many maximum cardinality. The second side is mandatory participation with one maximum cardinality.

This article uses relational semantics, not engine tuning. The examples are written in SQL-like form and use PostgreSQL-style constraints where convenient, but the modeling point is independent of indexes, optimizer choices, or physical design.
bullets: Cardinality: the maximum number of related rows allowed.
Participation: the minimum number of related rows required.
A complete relationship statement includes both sides: left min..max and right min..max.
A foreign key alone does not describe every participation rule in the conceptual model.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail model
paragraphs: Assume a small hypothetical retail-order dataset with customers, orders, order items, products, and customer profiles. The business rules are deliberately small enough to inspect by hand.

The first relationship is Customer to RetailOrder. A customer may have placed no orders yet, or may have placed many orders. Every order must belong to exactly one customer. Written as min..max: Customer 0..* to RetailOrder 1..1.

The second relationship is RetailOrder to OrderItem. Every order must contain at least one item. Every item belongs to exactly one order. Written as min..max: RetailOrder 1..* to OrderItem 1..1. This rule is more interesting because the mandatory side points from parent to child: the parent row is not complete unless at least one child row exists.

The third relationship is Customer to CustomerProfile. A customer may have no profile, but may not have more than one. Every profile belongs to exactly one customer. Written as min..max: Customer 0..1 to CustomerProfile 1..1.

The fourth relationship is Product to OrderItem. A product may appear in zero or many order items. Every order item must identify exactly one product. Written as min..max: Product 0..* to OrderItem 1..1.
bullets: Customer 0..* to RetailOrder 1..1: optional participation for customers, mandatory participation for orders.
RetailOrder 1..* to OrderItem 1..1: mandatory participation on both sides, with many items allowed per order.
Customer 0..1 to CustomerProfile 1..1: at most one profile per customer, and no orphan profile.
Product 0..* to OrderItem 1..1: products can exist before they sell, but order items cannot exist without a product.

sections.heading: What the relational constraints enforce
paragraphs: The DDL above enforces several relationship rules directly. The NOT NULL foreign key on retail_order.customer_id says an order must name a customer. The referenced primary key says the named customer must exist. Together they enforce the RetailOrder 1..1 side of Customer to RetailOrder.

The model also allows many orders per customer because customer_id is not unique in retail_order. If a unique constraint were added to retail_order.customer_id, the design would accidentally become Customer 0..1 to RetailOrder 1..1. That would reject a second order from the same customer, contradicting the intended rule.

The customer_profile table uses customer_id as both primary key and foreign key. That pattern enforces at most one profile per customer, because the primary key permits only one row for a given customer_id. It also enforces that every profile belongs to an existing customer. It does not require every customer to have a profile; that is intentional in this example.

The order_item primary key allows several lines per order because line_no varies within order_id. The NOT NULL foreign key to retail_order enforces that each item belongs to one existing order. The NOT NULL foreign key to product enforces that each item names one existing product.

One rule is not fully enforced by these ordinary row-level constraints: every order must have at least one item. The foreign key from order_item to retail_order prevents orphan items. It does not prevent a parent order from existing with no children. That is the common trap: a child-to-parent mandatory rule is easy to express with NOT NULL plus foreign key; a parent-to-child mandatory rule usually needs a different lifecycle control, validation query, deferred constraint mechanism, trigger, stored procedure, or application transaction boundary.
bullets: NOT NULL on a foreign key expresses mandatory participation from child to parent.
A non-unique foreign key permits many children for the same parent.
A UNIQUE constraint or primary key on a foreign key can express at-most-one on the child table.
A plain foreign key does not guarantee that every parent has at least one child.

sections.heading: Counterexamples in the data
paragraphs: Counterexamples make the distinction visible. The following rows are hypothetical and are meant as a staging or review fixture, not as a claim about any real retailer. Some rows should be accepted by the model; others illustrate specific violations.

Customers 1, 2, and 3 are valid customers. Customer 1 has two orders, which is allowed because the relationship is one customer to many orders. Customer 3 has no orders, which is also allowed because customer participation in orders is optional in this example.

Order 103 has a missing customer_id. That violates mandatory participation from RetailOrder to Customer. Order 104 references customer 999, which is also invalid because the required parent does not exist. Order 101 has no order items. That violates the business rule RetailOrder 1..* to OrderItem, even though a simple order table row could exist unless the load process prevents it.

The duplicate profile for customer 1 violates the at-most-one side of Customer 0..1 to CustomerProfile. A profile for customer 4 violates the mandatory parent rule for profiles, because there is no customer 4 in the customer table.
bullets: Valid: customer 1 has orders 100 and 101.
Valid: customer 3 has zero orders.
Invalid: order 103 has no customer.
Invalid: order 104 references a non-existent customer.
Invalid: order 101 has zero items.
Invalid: customer 1 has two profile rows.
Invalid: customer profile 4 has no matching customer.

INSERT INTO customer (customer_id, customer_name) VALUES
    (1, 'Asha'),
    (2, 'Ben'),
    (3, 'Cy');

INSERT INTO product (product_id, sku, product_name) VALUES
    (10, 'MUG-BLUE', 'Blue mug'),
    (11, 'TEA-250G', 'Tea 250g');

INSERT INTO retail_order (order_id, customer_id, placed_at) VALUES
    (100, 1, timestamp '2026-09-28 09:00:00'),
    (101, 1, timestamp '2026-09-28 09:05:00'),
    (102, 2, timestamp '2026-09-28 09:10:00');

INSERT INTO order_item (order_id, line_no, product_id, quantity) VALUES
    (100, 1, 10, 1),
    (100, 2, 11, 2),
    (102, 1, 10, 1);

    (1, 'asha@example.invalid', timestamp '2026-09-28 08:00:00'),
    (2, 'ben@example.invalid', timestamp '2026-09-28 08:10:00');

sections.heading: Diagnostic queries for staging and audits
paragraphs: In a production schema with enforced constraints, some violations cannot persist. In staging tables, lakehouse bronze tables, imports, reverse-engineering exercises, and data contracts, diagnostics are still useful. They make the intended relationship semantics executable as checks.

The first diagnostic finds orders that do not have exactly one valid customer. In a constrained relational table, NOT NULL plus foreign key should prevent these rows. In staging data, the query makes the rule explicit.

The second diagnostic finds orders with no items. This is the parent-to-child mandatory participation rule that ordinary foreign keys do not fully capture. If the business rule says an order is not valid until it has at least one item, this query identifies incomplete orders.

The third diagnostic finds customers with more than one profile in a staging table. In the final schema, customer_profile.customer_id as a primary key prevents duplicates. In raw data, grouping by customer_id exposes the violation before loading.

These diagnostics should not be confused with performance recommendations. A large system may need indexes, partition-aware checks, incremental validation, or data quality tooling. Those choices belong to physical implementation. The modeling step is to state the rule precisely enough that any implementation can be judged against it.

codeExamples.code:
SELECT
    o.order_id,
    o.customer_id
FROM retail_order AS o
LEFT JOIN customer AS c
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL
   OR c.customer_id IS NULL;

SELECT
    o.order_id
FROM retail_order AS o
LEFT JOIN order_item AS i
    ON i.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.order_id
HAVING COUNT(i.order_id) = 0;

SELECT
    customer_id,
    COUNT(*) AS profile_count
FROM customer_profile_staging
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

sections.heading: A checklist for specifying both constraints
paragraphs: A practical model review can be short. For each relationship, name the two entities, choose the parent and child if the relationship is directional in the schema, then write min..max on both sides. Do not stop at one-to-many. The minimum is where many production data quality surprises hide.

Next, classify which parts are enforceable with ordinary relational constraints. Primary keys identify rows. Foreign keys require referenced parents. NOT NULL makes a reference mandatory. UNIQUE and primary key constraints limit multiplicity. CHECK constraints handle row-local facts such as positive quantity, but they do not count related rows in another table.

Finally, decide how to handle rules that cross rows or require existence of children. For an order that must have at least one item, common choices include creating orders and items in the same transaction, preventing an order from reaching a submitted status until lines exist, using a deferred database mechanism, or running a validation job before publishing curated data. The right choice depends on lifecycle semantics, not just DDL elegance.

The most important modeling habit is to state the intended valid and invalid examples. If the team cannot agree whether customer 3 with zero orders is valid, or whether order 101 with zero items is valid, the diagram is not specific enough.
bullets: Write each relationship as EntityA min..max to EntityB min..max.
Translate maximum one into primary key or unique constraints where appropriate.
Translate mandatory child-to-parent participation into NOT NULL foreign keys.
Do not assume a foreign key from child to parent proves that every parent has a child.
Keep counterexamples with the model so reviewers can see what should be rejected.

takeaways: Cardinality and participation are separate constraints: maximum allowed related rows and minimum required related rows.
NOT NULL foreign keys are strong for mandatory child-to-parent relationships, but they do not by themselves enforce that every parent has at least one child.
A small counterexample dataset is an effective way to validate whether a model really specifies one-to-one, one-to-many, optional, and mandatory rules.
Use primary keys, foreign keys, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, and CHECK constraints where they match the rule; use lifecycle controls or validation for cross-row participation rules.

title: Weak entities and identifying relationships
description: A practical guide to modeling records whose identity depends on a parent record, using a hypothetical retail order dataset and counterexamples that show when a child table is, and is not, a weak entity.
lead: Some records cannot be named correctly without another record. An order line is often line 1, line 2, or line 3 only within a specific order. A room number may be unique only within a hotel. A subscription phase may be sequence 1 only within a subscription. These are the cases where weak entities and identifying relationships are useful: the child record’s identity includes the parent’s identity, not just a reference to it.

sections.heading: The modeling problem: a child row that is not globally identifiable
paragraphs: A weak entity is an entity whose rows are identified through another entity. In relational terms, the child table does not have a complete natural identifier by itself. It has a local discriminator, such as line_number, room_number, or sequence_number, but that discriminator only works inside the scope of a parent row. The identifying relationship is the relationship that brings the parent’s key into the child’s identifier.

This is not the same as saying every child table is weak. Many child tables have foreign keys to parent tables while still having their own independent identity. For example, a shipment may reference an order, but if shipment_id is a stable business identifier used by carriers, support agents, and downstream integrations, then the shipment can be identified without combining it with order_id. It depends on the order in the process sense, but not necessarily in the identifier sense.

The practical question is: what values would a person or system need to distinguish one row from another without ambiguity? If the answer is parent key plus a local value, you probably have a weak entity. If the answer is a stable key that is meaningful outside the parent, you probably have a regular entity with a foreign key.

This topic assumes you are already comfortable with candidate keys. The important step is to name the candidate keys before choosing columns for primary keys. If a supposed child table has a true candidate key independent of the parent, model that explicitly. If it does not, do not pretend that a local sequence number is globally unique.

sections.heading: Worked example: hypothetical retail orders and order lines
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail dataset with order headers and order lines. The order has an order_id. Each line has a line_number that starts over at 1 for every order. A user interface may display an order as 9001 line 1, 9001 line 2, and so on. The phrase line 1 alone is not enough to identify a row, because many orders have a line 1.
Here is a small fixture. The data is hypothetical and intentionally tiny so the identity problem is visible.
bullets: Order 9001 has line 1 for SKU MUG-BLUE and line 2 for SKU TEA-250G.
Order 9002 has line 1 for SKU MUG-BLUE.
Order 9003 has line 1 for SKU CARD-BDAY and line 2 for SKU CARD-BDAY because the same SKU was added in two separate promotions.

sections.heading: Check the functional dependencies before drawing the tables
paragraphs: A useful way to verify the model is to state the functional dependencies. In this example, order_id determines order-level facts such as order_date and customer_id. The pair order_id and line_number determines line-level facts such as sku, quantity, and unit_price_cents. The line_number by itself determines nothing outside a single order. The sku by itself also does not identify the order line, because the same SKU can appear on multiple orders and can even appear more than once on the same order.

The relevant dependency is: order_id, line_number determines sku, quantity, unit_price_cents. That makes order line a weak entity in this model. Its identifier is not line_number. Its identifier is the composite of the parent key and the local discriminator.

This also shows a common normalization boundary. Do not store order_date or customer_id in the order_line table just because most queries need those values. Those attributes depend on order_id, not on the full composite key order_id plus line_number. Keeping order-level facts on the order table and line-level facts on the line table prevents the line table from mixing two grains.

sections.heading: Relational implementation with an identifying relationship
paragraphs: In a relational schema, the identifying relationship is represented by including the parent key in the child table’s primary key and also declaring it as a foreign key to the parent table. The child’s primary key is composite: order_id plus line_number. The order_id column is not merely a navigational reference; it participates in the child row’s identity.

The following SQL is illustrative. It uses common constraint patterns: primary keys, foreign keys, uniqueness, and simple checks. Syntax details can vary by database, so a publisher should validate it in the target engine before treating it as executable reference code.

codeExamples.code:
INSERT INTO customer (customer_id, email) VALUES
    (501, 'customer501@example.test'),
    (502, 'customer502@example.test');

INSERT INTO order_header (order_id, customer_id, order_date) VALUES
    (9001, 501, DATE '2026-09-01'),
    (9002, 502, DATE '2026-09-01'),
    (9003, 501, DATE '2026-09-02');

INSERT INTO order_line (order_id, line_number, sku, quantity, unit_price_cents) VALUES
    (9001, 1, 'MUG-BLUE', 2, 1299),
    (9001, 2, 'TEA-250G', 1, 899),
    (9002, 1, 'MUG-BLUE', 1, 1299),
    (9003, 1, 'CARD-BDAY', 1, 399),
    (9003, 2, 'CARD-BDAY', 1, 0);

sections.heading: Counterexamples that look plausible but weaken the model
paragraphs: The first counterexample is using line_number as the primary key. That fails immediately because line_number repeats across orders. The database would reject valid rows such as order 9001 line 1 and order 9002 line 1 if line_number alone were declared unique. If the database does not enforce uniqueness, then line_number cannot serve as an identifier at all.

The second counterexample is using order_id plus sku as the primary key. That may work in a simplified demo, but the hypothetical order 9003 shows why it is unsafe. The same SKU appears twice on the same order with different prices because one unit came from a promotion. If the business permits split shipments, partial discounts, substitutions, or separate fulfillment groups, SKU often describes what was purchased; it does not necessarily identify the line.

The third counterexample is adding a surrogate order_line_id and stopping there. A surrogate key can be useful for operational convenience, especially when many downstream tables need to reference one line. But if the business rule says an order cannot have two line 1 rows, the schema still needs a unique constraint on order_id plus line_number. Without that constraint, the surrogate key hides duplicate business identifiers rather than resolving them.

codeExamples.code:
-- Counterexample: this rejects valid data because line_number repeats across orders.
CREATE TABLE bad_order_line_by_line_number (
    line_number        integer PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id           bigint NOT NULL,
    sku                varchar(64) NOT NULL
);

-- Counterexample: this rejects valid data when the same SKU appears twice on one order.
CREATE TABLE bad_order_line_by_sku (
    order_id           bigint NOT NULL,
    sku                varchar(64) NOT NULL,
    quantity           integer NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, sku)
);

-- Sometimes acceptable, but incomplete if it omits the business uniqueness rule.
CREATE TABLE order_line_with_surrogate (
    order_line_id      bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id           bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES order_header (order_id),
    line_number        integer NOT NULL,
    sku                varchar(64) NOT NULL,
    quantity           integer NOT NULL,
    UNIQUE (order_id, line_number)
);

sections.heading: A diagnostic for identifying weak entities
paragraphs: When reviewing a model, ask these questions in order. First, can a row be named without any parent value? If not, the entity may be weak. Second, does the child have a local discriminator whose values repeat under different parents? If yes, the parent key probably belongs in the child identifier. Third, are attributes placed at the correct grain? If a column depends only on the parent key, keep it on the parent. If it depends on the parent key plus child discriminator, keep it on the child.

Fourth, decide whether a surrogate key changes the logical model or only the physical reference pattern. A surrogate key does not make a weak entity strong by itself. It gives the row another handle, but it does not replace the need to enforce the natural business identifier if that identifier matters. A table can have a surrogate primary key and still have an identifying business constraint, but the model should make that choice explicit.

Finally, watch for overuse. Some structures are hierarchical without being weak entities in the same sense. A category tree, an employee management chain, or a variable-depth product taxonomy may involve parent-child references, but each node may still have its own stable identifier. In that case, the parent relationship describes placement in a hierarchy, not necessarily the row’s identity. Hierarchy design has its own modeling choices and should not be collapsed into the weak-entity pattern automatically.
bullets: Use a weak entity when the child’s meaningful identifier is parent key plus local discriminator.
Do not use a weak entity just because the table has a foreign key.
If you add a surrogate key, still enforce the parent-scoped candidate key when the business depends on it.

sections.heading: Tradeoffs and boundaries
paragraphs: Composite keys make the dependency visible. They also make downstream foreign keys wider: any table that references an order line must carry both order_id and line_number. That can be a good thing when the parent context is essential, because joins and constraints preserve the real identifier. It can also be inconvenient when many tables reference the child row and the composite key becomes repetitive.

Surrogate keys make references narrower, but they can make the model less self-explanatory if they replace rather than supplement the parent-scoped business key. A balanced design is often to use a surrogate key for mechanical references and a unique constraint for the identifying business rule. The right choice depends on how the data is created, how users talk about records, and how often other tables must point to the child.

The scope here is relational semantics, not query tuning. Index choices, clustering, partitioning, and engine-specific performance behavior should be evaluated separately. The semantic requirement is simpler: if a record’s identity depends on a parent entity, represent that dependency as part of the candidate key or as a separately enforced uniqueness rule.

takeaways: A weak entity is identified through its parent; in a relational schema, that usually means the parent key participates in the child’s candidate key.
An identifying relationship is stronger than an ordinary foreign-key reference because the parent key helps identify the child row, not merely connect to it.
Surrogate keys can be practical, but they do not remove the need to enforce the parent-scoped business identifier when that identifier is part of the data’s meaning.
Counterexamples are useful: test whether a proposed key rejects valid data, allows duplicate business identifiers, or places attributes at the wrong grain.

title: Associative entities for many-to-many relationships
description: A practical guide to modeling many-to-many relationships without losing attributes that belong to the relationship itself.
lead: When two entity tables have a many-to-many relationship, the tempting shortcut is to flatten one side into the other. That shortcut fails as soon as the relationship has its own facts: dates, roles, quantities, statuses, prices, permissions, or codes. An associative entity turns the relationship into a table with its own key, foreign keys, and attributes, so the model preserves what actually happened instead of smearing relationship facts across unrelated entities.

sections.heading: The modeling problem: relationship facts are not entity facts
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail marketing dataset. The business has customers and offers. A customer can receive many offers, and the same offer can be sent to many customers. That is already a many-to-many relationship. The important part is that the relationship has its own attributes.

For example, customer C001 receives offer O10 by email on 2026-09-01 with coupon code SAVE10-A7. Customer C002 receives the same offer by SMS on 2026-09-02 with coupon code SAVE10-K3. The offer name, offer start date, and offer description belong to the offer. The customer email address and loyalty status belong to the customer. But sent_at, channel, coupon_code, and redeemed_at belong to the assignment of a particular offer to a particular customer.

If those relationship attributes are pushed into the customer table, the customer row becomes a repeating group of offer columns. If they are pushed into the offer table, the offer row becomes a repeating group of customer columns. If both entities are flattened into one wide table, customer attributes and offer attributes are duplicated across rows, and every update becomes ambiguous: are you changing the customer, the offer, or one delivery of the offer to one customer?

An associative entity solves this by making the relationship explicit. Instead of modeling only customer and offer, add customer_offer. That table represents one customer receiving one offer under a defined set of assumptions. Its key identifies the relationship occurrence. Its foreign keys point to the participating entities. Its non-key columns describe facts about that occurrence.
bullets: Entity fact: customer C001 has loyalty tier Gold.
Entity fact: offer O10 is named Fall Welcome Credit.
Relationship fact: customer C001 received offer O10 by email on 2026-09-01.
Relationship fact: customer C001 redeemed offer O10 on 2026-09-04 with coupon code SAVE10-A7.

sections.heading: Counterexample: flattening creates update and meaning problems
paragraphs: A common first attempt is to add offer columns to the customer table. That looks acceptable while each customer has one offer. It breaks when the second offer arrives.

In the following hypothetical flat structure, offer data and relationship data are mixed into customer rows. The table can only store two offers unless more columns are added. Queries must know which numbered column to inspect. Constraints such as one coupon code per offer assignment become awkward because the same concept is split across multiple columns.
bullets: customer_id: C001
customer_email: ada@example.test
loyalty_tier: Gold
offer_1_id: O10
offer_1_sent_at: 2026-09-01
offer_1_channel: email
offer_1_coupon_code: SAVE10-A7
offer_2_id: O20
offer_2_sent_at: 2026-09-09
offer_2_channel: sms
offer_2_coupon_code: SHIP5-Q2

sections.heading: Why the flat shape fails
paragraphs: The first failure is repeating structure. The model has offer_1 and offer_2 columns, but the business rule is not really two offers per customer. The business rule is zero or more offer assignments per customer. A relational design should model that set directly rather than reserve numbered slots.

The second failure is dependency confusion. Normalization is concerned with dependencies between keys and attributes: a fact should be stored where it depends on the key. In the flat customer row, loyalty_tier depends on customer_id. Offer name depends on offer_id. Coupon code depends on the assignment of an offer to a customer. Those are three different determinants, but the flattened table stores them in one row as if customer_id alone determined everything.

The third failure is update ambiguity. Suppose offer O10 is renamed from Fall Welcome Credit to Fall Member Credit. If the offer name has been copied onto every customer row that received the offer, every copy must be updated consistently. If one row is missed, the database now says the same offer has two names. The error came from storing an offer attribute inside repeated customer-offer occurrences.

The fourth failure is lost relationship history. If C001 receives O10 twice in two separate campaign waves, the candidate key may not be only customer_id plus offer_id. The relationship occurrence may need its own identifier or a broader key such as customer_id, offer_id, and sent_at. A flattened table usually hides that question until data arrives that does not fit.

sections.heading: Design the associative entity
paragraphs: Start with the two base entities. In this hypothetical example, customer stores customer-level facts and offer stores offer-level facts. Then add customer_offer for the relationship occurrence.

The important design decision is the grain of customer_offer. A useful grain statement is: one row represents one assignment of one offer to one customer. Under the simplifying assumption that the same offer is assigned to the same customer at most once, the pair customer_id and offer_id can be the primary key. If the same offer can be assigned to the same customer multiple times, use a separate customer_offer_id as the primary key and enforce a different alternate key that matches the business rule, such as customer_id, offer_id, and sent_at.

The associative entity is not just a join table with two foreign keys. A pure join table records membership in a relationship. An associative entity records membership plus facts about that relationship. In practice, the difference matters because relationship facts need the same modeling care as entity facts: keys, nullability, uniqueness, valid states, and clear ownership.
bullets: customer.customer_id determines customer attributes such as email and loyalty_tier.
offer.offer_id determines offer attributes such as offer_name and offer_type.
customer_offer.customer_id plus customer_offer.offer_id determines assignment attributes such as sent_at, channel, coupon_code, and redeemed_at under the one-assignment assumption.

codeExamples.code:
CREATE TABLE customer (
    customer_id      VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    email_address    VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    loyalty_tier     VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE offer (
    offer_id         VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    offer_name       VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    offer_type       VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE customer_offer (
    customer_id      VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    offer_id         VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    sent_at          TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    channel          VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    coupon_code      VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    redeemed_at      TIMESTAMP NULL,

    PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, offer_id),
    UNIQUE (coupon_code),

    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customer (customer_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (offer_id) REFERENCES offer (offer_id),

    CHECK (redeemed_at IS NULL OR redeemed_at >= sent_at)
);

sections.heading: Worked example with hypothetical data
paragraphs: Here is a small data fixture using the one-assignment assumption. The customers are C001 and C002. The offers are O10 and O20. The associative entity records which customer received which offer and the facts about that assignment.
Customer rows: C001 has email ada@example.test and loyalty tier Gold. C002 has email ben@example.test and loyalty tier Silver.
Offer rows: O10 is Fall Welcome Credit with type discount. O20 is Free Shipping Nudge with type shipping.

Customer-offer rows: C001 received O10 by email on 2026-09-01 with coupon SAVE10-A7 and redeemed it on 2026-09-04. C001 received O20 by SMS on 2026-09-09 with coupon SHIP5-Q2 and has not redeemed it. C002 received O10 by SMS on 2026-09-02 with coupon SAVE10-K3 and has not redeemed it.

This shape answers questions without duplicating entity facts. To count how many customers received O10, query customer_offer where offer_id equals O10. To list all offers sent to C001, query customer_offer where customer_id equals C001 and join to offer for names. To change C001’s loyalty tier, update one customer row. To rename O10, update one offer row. To mark a redemption, update the one relationship row for the relevant customer and offer.

The model also preserves meaning when the same offer has different outcomes for different customers. O10 is the same offer for C001 and C002, but the channel, coupon code, sent date, and redemption status differ. Those differences are not customer facts in isolation and not offer facts in isolation. They are facts about the pairing.

codeExamples.code:
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.email_address,
    o.offer_name,
    co.sent_at,
    co.channel,
    co.coupon_code,
    co.redeemed_at
FROM customer_offer co
JOIN customer c
    ON c.customer_id = co.customer_id
JOIN offer o
    ON o.offer_id = co.offer_id
WHERE co.customer_id = 'C001'
ORDER BY co.sent_at;

sections.heading: Choose the key from the relationship grain
paragraphs: The most common mistake is to choose the key before stating the grain. For an associative entity, the key should identify one relationship occurrence. Sometimes the two parent keys are enough. Sometimes they are not.

Use a composite primary key such as customer_id plus offer_id when the business rule is exactly one relationship row for that pair. This is compact and makes duplicate assignments impossible at the key level. It also makes child references longer if other tables must refer to a specific assignment.

Use a surrogate key such as customer_offer_id when the relationship has a life of its own, when other tables refer to it, or when the same pair can occur more than once. In that case, do not stop at adding the surrogate key. Add an alternate key or uniqueness rule for the natural business identifier. Otherwise the model permits accidental duplicates because every row has a different surrogate value.

For example, if the business can send the same offer to the same customer in multiple waves, customer_id plus offer_id is not unique. A better grain statement may be: one row represents one send of one offer to one customer at one sent_at timestamp. The candidate key might then be customer_id, offer_id, and sent_at, assuming sent_at is precise and governed enough to distinguish sends. If not, a campaign_wave_id or delivery_id may be a better determinant.
bullets: Ask whether the same two parent records can be related more than once.
Ask whether the relationship has attributes that change independently from both parent entities.
Ask whether downstream tables need to reference the relationship occurrence itself.
Ask which columns a business user would use to identify a duplicate relationship row.

codeExamples.code:
CREATE TABLE customer_offer_send (
    customer_offer_send_id  BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id             VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    offer_id                VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    sent_at                 TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    channel                 VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    coupon_code             VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    redeemed_at             TIMESTAMP NULL,

    UNIQUE (customer_id, offer_id, sent_at),
    UNIQUE (coupon_code),

    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customer (customer_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (offer_id) REFERENCES offer (offer_id),

    CHECK (redeemed_at IS NULL OR redeemed_at >= sent_at)
);

sections.heading: A diagnostic for relationship attributes
paragraphs: When reviewing a model, look for columns whose meaning includes two nouns. If a column name or definition sounds like customer’s offer channel, product’s supplier cost, user’s account role, student’s course grade, or order’s product quantity, it is probably describing a relationship. That does not automatically prove it needs a separate associative entity, but it is a strong signal.

A second diagnostic is update scope. If changing one value requires updating many copied rows, the attribute is probably stored at the wrong grain. If a value can differ for the same customer across offers, it is not solely a customer attribute. If it can differ for the same offer across customers, it is not solely an offer attribute.

A third diagnostic is cardinality pressure. Numbered columns such as product_1, product_2, product_3 or offer_1_date, offer_2_date often indicate a many-to-many relationship forced into a one-row shape. Arrays and delimited lists can hide the same issue. They may be acceptable for ingestion staging or document storage, but they are usually poor relational representations when the individual relationships must be queried, constrained, or audited.

Finally, separate the relational model from a reporting projection. Analysts may need a denormalized table for a dashboard, feature set, or export. That does not mean the durable relational model should store customer, offer, and assignment facts in one table. Build the associative entity first, then derive flattened outputs when a consumer needs them.
bullets: Does the attribute depend on one entity key, or on a combination of entity keys?
Can the same pair of entities occur more than once?
Would deleting one parent row leave relationship facts with no meaning?
Are numbered columns or repeated groups standing in for rows?
Can constraints express the business rule clearly in the current shape?

takeaways: Use an associative entity when a many-to-many relationship has its own attributes, not just when you need a technical join table.
State the relationship grain before choosing the key; the two parent keys are sufficient only when the pair can occur once under the business rules.
Flattened tables often mix entity facts with relationship facts, causing duplication, ambiguous updates, and lost history.
Relationship attributes should be constrained at the relationship grain, where foreign keys, uniqueness rules, and checks can express the intended semantics.
