title: Database constraints versus validation queries
description: A practical guide for deciding which data rules belong in database constraints and which belong in validation queries, using a small hypothetical retail dataset with counterexamples.
lead: A validation query can tell you that bad data exists. A database constraint can prevent certain bad data from being committed in the first place. Treating those as interchangeable is a common modeling mistake. The practical question is not whether constraints or validation queries are better; it is which invariants must be enforced synchronously, and which possible violations can only be observed asynchronously.

sections.heading: The distinction that matters
paragraphs: A database constraint is part of the definition of a relation. It says, in effect, that some database state is not allowed. If a row would violate a primary key, foreign key, not-null rule, unique constraint, or check constraint, the database rejects the change. The bad state does not become visible as normal committed data.

A validation query is different. It reads data that already exists and returns rows that look suspicious, inconsistent, incomplete, or contrary to a business rule. It is an observation mechanism, not an enforcement mechanism. The query may run every hour, every day, before a publish step, or during a reconciliation workflow. Until it runs and someone or something responds, the violation can already affect downstream consumers.

That difference matters for data engineers because many data quality failures are misclassified. Teams sometimes use validation queries for rules that should have been enforced as relational invariants. The result is avoidable damage: orphaned facts, duplicate keys, impossible quantities, and other states that downstream models must defensively handle forever. The opposite mistake also happens: teams try to encode every operational expectation as a database constraint, even when the rule depends on time, delayed events, external systems, or a remediation process.
A useful decision rule is: enforce what makes the relation invalid by definition; validate what makes the current state suspicious, incomplete, or operationally out of policy.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail schema with enforced invariants
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail order model. The core relations are customers, products, orders, and order lines. This example is intentionally small, but it is enough to separate rules that the database can enforce from rules that should be checked asynchronously.

The following definition expresses several invariants. A customer must have an email. A product must have a stock keeping unit. An order must reference an existing customer. An order line must reference an existing order and product. Quantity must be positive. A line number cannot repeat within the same order.

These rules are not merely quality preferences. If an order line refers to a product that does not exist in the modeled product relation, the line is not relationally well-formed. If quantity is negative, the row does not represent the intended kind of order line. If two rows share the same order_id and line_number, the model no longer has a stable way to identify one line within an order.
bullets: Use constraints when the rule defines whether a row or relationship is valid at all.
Prefer constraints when the rule can be decided at write time using the row and referenced keys.
Use validation queries when the rule requires observation across delayed facts, aggregates, event timing, or external business processes.

sections.heading: What constraints prevent
paragraphs: Suppose a load process tries to insert an order line with product_id 9999, but no product row has product_id 9999. With the foreign key in place, the database rejects the insert. The validation query for orphaned order lines never needs to find this case in the final table, because the invalid relationship is not allowed to exist there.

Now suppose the load process tries to insert quantity = 0 for an order line. The check constraint rejects it. Downstream logic does not need to decide whether zero means a free sample, a deleted line, a failed ingestion mapping, or an accidental default. If zero-quantity lines are meaningful in the business process, then the constraint is wrong and the model should represent that meaning explicitly. But if an order line means a purchased quantity of a product, quantity > 0 belongs in the schema.

The important point is not that every database engine has identical constraint behavior or syntax. The important modeling point is that constraints are synchronous guards on allowed states. PostgreSQL documents constraints such as check constraints, not-null constraints, unique constraints, primary keys, and foreign keys as mechanisms for defining data rules at the table level. Other relational systems expose similar concepts, although details vary.

A counterexample makes the distinction clearer. Imagine choosing not to define the product foreign key and instead scheduling this query once per day: select order lines whose product_id is missing from product. That query may be useful in a staging area. It is a poor substitute for an invariant in the final order_line table. During the day, dashboards, marts, and exports can all read the orphaned line as if it were valid. By the time the query reports the problem, the bad state has already propagated.

codeExamples.code:
-- Diagnostic query that should return no rows in a properly constrained final table.
-- Useful as a safety check, but not a substitute for the foreign key.
SELECT ol.order_id, ol.line_number, ol.product_id
FROM order_line AS ol
LEFT JOIN product AS p
  ON p.product_id = ol.product_id
WHERE p.product_id IS NULL;

sections.heading: What validation queries observe
paragraphs: Some rules are not good constraint candidates, even when they are important. They may depend on a sequence of events, a tolerance threshold, an external payment provider, or a business workflow where temporary inconsistency is expected. In those cases, a validation query is the right instrument because the purpose is to identify exceptions, not to declare the entire relation impossible.

Extend the hypothetical retail model with payment and shipment events. A payment references an order. A shipment references an order. Basic structure can still be constrained: payment amount cannot be negative, payment status must be from an allowed set, and each event must reference an existing order. But higher-level expectations require observation.

For example, a paid order should usually have at least one line. The charged amount should usually equal the sum of line quantities multiplied by unit prices. A shipment should not usually occur before the order was placed. Those are real data quality checks, but they are not the same kind of rule as quantity > 0. They compare multiple relations, aggregate line items, or interpret event timing. They may also have legitimate exceptions: a partial capture, a manual adjustment, a replacement shipment, or an order imported from an older system with incomplete event history.

Validation queries are well suited for these cases because they produce exception sets. The output should be operationally useful: order_id, the observed values, the expected values, and enough context to route the issue.

sections.heading: Worked validation exceptions
paragraphs: The next query calculates three exception types over the hypothetical schema. It is written as a diagnostic pattern rather than a claim that every retail system should use these exact rules.

The first branch finds paid orders with no order lines. The second compares captured payment amount with the computed order-line total. The third finds shipment events earlier than the order placement timestamp. Each branch returns rows that deserve investigation; it does not prove fraud, corruption, or a software defect by itself.

This distinction is important. A validation query produces candidates for review or remediation. It should be paired with an owner, severity, expected latency, and action. A daily query that nobody reads is documentation, not control. A validation query that blocks a publish step is stronger, but it is still asynchronous relative to the original write unless it runs in the same transaction as the change.

The query also illustrates why joins are central to validation. Table expressions and joins let you compare facts across relations: orders to lines, payments to computed totals, shipments to order timestamps. The relational operation is observation over current state. It does not retroactively prevent the bad state from having existed.

codeExamples.code:
WITH line_totals AS (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    SUM(quantity * unit_price_cents) AS line_total_cents,
    COUNT(*) AS line_count
  FROM order_line
  GROUP BY order_id
), captured_payments AS (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    SUM(amount_cents) AS captured_amount_cents
  FROM payment_event
  WHERE payment_status = 'captured'
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT
  'paid_order_without_lines' AS exception_type,
  o.order_id,
  NULL AS observed_cents,
  NULL AS expected_cents,
  'Paid order has no order_line rows' AS explanation
FROM retail_order AS o
LEFT JOIN line_totals AS lt
  ON lt.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_status = 'paid'
  AND COALESCE(lt.line_count, 0) = 0

UNION ALL

SELECT
  'captured_amount_mismatch' AS exception_type,
  o.order_id,
  cp.captured_amount_cents AS observed_cents,
  lt.line_total_cents AS expected_cents,
  'Captured payment total differs from order line total' AS explanation
FROM retail_order AS o
JOIN captured_payments AS cp
  ON cp.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN line_totals AS lt
  ON lt.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE cp.captured_amount_cents <> lt.line_total_cents

UNION ALL

SELECT
  'shipment_before_order_placed' AS exception_type,
  o.order_id,
  NULL AS observed_cents,
  NULL AS expected_cents,
  'Shipment event occurred before the order placement timestamp' AS explanation
FROM retail_order AS o
JOIN shipment_event AS se
  ON se.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE se.occurred_at < o.placed_at;

sections.heading: A decision framework for classifying rules
paragraphs: When a new data rule appears, classify it before implementing it. The classification prevents two common failures: under-enforcing structural invariants and over-constraining operational workflows.

Ask first whether the rule defines identity or referential meaning. Candidate keys, alternate keys, primary keys, and foreign keys usually belong in constraints when the modeled relationship is mandatory. If a final fact table says product_id, and product_id is supposed to refer to the product relation, enforce that reference. If the upstream feed can arrive before the product dimension, use a staging table, an unknown-product member, or a pending resolution workflow rather than weakening the final model without naming the tradeoff.

Ask next whether the rule can be evaluated at the moment of write. Not-null, check, uniqueness, and referential constraints are strong fits when the needed facts are available. Rules that require comparing today’s state with tomorrow’s file, waiting for a payment gateway, or reconciling a third-party shipment feed are usually validation checks.

Then ask whether violations are impossible or merely undesirable. Negative quantity may be impossible under the meaning of order_line. A captured amount that differs from the item total may be undesirable, but it might also reflect shipping charges, taxes, discounts, split tenders, manual credits, or a modeling omission. If legitimate exceptions exist, either refine the model so the invariant becomes precise, or keep the check as an exception report with categories.

Finally, decide what happens after detection. A constraint has a built-in consequence: reject the write. A validation query needs an operating model: alert, quarantine, backfill, annotate, suppress known exceptions, or block publication. Without that response path, the validation query only describes risk.
bullets: Constraint candidate: violation makes the row or relationship invalid by definition.
Validation candidate: violation is time-dependent, aggregate-dependent, external-system-dependent, or exception-prone.
Staging candidate: source data is allowed to be temporarily messy, but the curated relation should still enforce the invariant.

sections.heading: A practical pattern: stage, enforce, then validate
paragraphs: A robust data pipeline often uses all three layers. First, land source data with minimal assumptions in staging tables. Staging preserves evidence of what arrived, including malformed records. Second, transform into curated relational tables that enforce structural invariants. Third, run validation queries over curated data to detect business exceptions and reconciliation failures.

This pattern avoids turning final tables into unbounded error buckets. It also avoids pretending that every upstream irregularity can be solved with a check constraint. The staging layer absorbs source variability. The curated layer defines what valid relational data means. The validation layer watches for conditions that require investigation after the data becomes relationally well-formed.

For the hypothetical retail model, a staging table might accept raw order lines where product_sku is missing or quantity is a string. The curated order_line table should not. During transformation, rows that cannot be mapped to a valid product_id or positive integer quantity are rejected, quarantined, or assigned to an explicit exception workflow. Once rows enter order_line, downstream users can rely on its declared invariants.

Validation queries then handle higher-level questions: Does every paid order have lines? Do captured payments reconcile to modeled charges? Are shipment events temporally plausible? Are there orders stuck in draft for too long? These checks improve trust without weakening the core relational model.

sections.heading: Common misclassifications
paragraphs: One misclassification is using validation to replace a primary or foreign key. If a relationship is required by the model, an after-the-fact orphan check is not enough for the final table. It may still be useful as a defense-in-depth diagnostic, but it should not be the only guard.

Another misclassification is forcing uncertain business processes into rigid constraints too early. For example, shipment-before-payment may sound impossible until the business supports invoicing, subscriptions, replacements, or manual fulfillment. A premature constraint can reject legitimate records and encourage workarounds outside the model. In that case, write a validation query first, study the exception categories, and then promote the rule to a constraint only if the invariant becomes precise.

A third misclassification is hiding policy inside application code while leaving the database weaker than the model. If every application path assumes email is required, but the database allows null email in the customer relation, another loader or repair script can violate the assumption. Constraints put shared invariants where all writers must obey them.

The goal is not to maximize the number of constraints or validation queries. The goal is to make the contract explicit. Constraints define what cannot be stored as valid relational state. Validation queries define what stored state should be reviewed, reconciled, or improved.

takeaways: Use database constraints for enforced invariants: keys, required references, non-null facts, allowed domains, and checks that define whether a row or relationship is valid.
Use validation queries for asynchronously observed violations: aggregate mismatches, delayed events, temporal anomalies, reconciliation checks, and exception-prone business policies.
Do not use a scheduled validation query as the only protection for a final-table invariant that the database can enforce synchronously.
A good validation query returns actionable exception rows, not just a count. Include identifiers, observed values, expected values, and a clear exception type.
A practical pipeline separates staging tolerance, curated-table enforcement, and validation-based monitoring.

title: Uniqueness with nullable business identifiers
description: A practical guide to defining duplicate rules when an external business identifier is missing, using a small hypothetical customer dataset with counterexamples.
lead: Nullable business identifiers create a modeling trap: two missing identifiers do not mean two rows identify the same thing. The useful question is not whether NULLs are equal, but which evidence is strong enough to declare, reject, or defer a duplicate decision.

sections.heading: The problem with missing identifiers
paragraphs: A business identifier is useful because it narrows the duplicate rule. If customer_id from the web store is present and the source system promises that it identifies one customer, then two rows with the same source system and customer_id can be treated as the same business entity for that source. That does not solve every identity problem, but it gives the data model a candidate key or alternate key to reason about.

The hard case is the row where the external identifier is missing. A common mistake is to let the nullable identifier participate in a uniqueness rule as if missing were a value. That turns an absence of evidence into evidence of sameness. Two imported customer rows with NULL external_customer_id might be the same customer, two different customers, or two incomplete records that cannot be decided yet.

Relationally, NULL represents an unknown or inapplicable value, not a known shared value. PostgreSQL’s documentation on constraints is a useful reminder that unique constraints and null values have specific database semantics, and those semantics are not the same thing as a business duplicate policy. This article stays at the modeling level: what rule should a practitioner write down before deciding how to enforce or observe it.
bullets: Do not define duplicates as external_customer_id is equal, including when both sides are NULL.
Do scope external identifiers to the system or domain that issued them unless the business has a verified global identifier.
Do define fallback evidence separately from the primary identifier, with an explicit outcome for ambiguous matches.

sections.heading: A hypothetical customer fixture with counterexamples
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail customer staging table. The rows are deliberately small, but they include the failure modes that make nullable business identifiers tricky.

The assumed business context is this: source_system plus external_customer_id is a reliable identifier when both are present. Email plus last name is acceptable fallback evidence only for records with a missing external identifier, unless it collides with multiple known external identifiers. Phone plus postal code plus last name is weaker fallback evidence and is used only when email is missing. These are not universal rules; they are example rules chosen to make the modeling decision concrete.

The fixture includes four different outcomes. Rows 1 and 2 are duplicates by the issued external identifier even though the email changed. Row 3 is missing the identifier but has fallback evidence pointing to the known C100 customer. Rows 4 and 5 show why fallback evidence must not override two different known identifiers: the same shared email, phone, postal code, and last name might represent a household, a reused email, a data entry error, or a true duplicate, but the model should not collapse C200 and C201 automatically. Row 6 is missing the identifier and matches that ambiguous fallback key, so it cannot be safely assigned. Rows 8 and 9 are provisional duplicates among missing-identifier rows. Row 10 has too little evidence to decide.

codeExamples.code:
WITH customer_stage (
    row_id,
    source_system,
    external_customer_id,
    email_norm,
    phone_e164,
    postal_code,
    last_name_norm
) AS (
    VALUES
        (1,  'web',   'C100', 'ada@example.test',    '+1555010100', '02139', 'lovelace'),
        (2,  'web',   'C100', 'ada.new@example.test','+1555010100', '02139', 'lovelace'),
        (3,  'web',   NULL,   'ada@example.test',    '+1555010100', '02139', 'lovelace'),
        (4,  'web',   'C200', 'shared@example.test', '+1555010101', '10001', 'chen'),
        (5,  'web',   'C201', 'shared@example.test', '+1555010101', '10001', 'chen'),
        (6,  'web',   NULL,   'shared@example.test', '+1555010101', '10001', 'chen'),
        (7,  'store', 'C100', 'ada@example.test',    '+1555010100', '02139', 'lovelace'),
        (8,  'web',   NULL,   NULL,                  '+1555010200', '60601', 'patel'),
        (9,  'web',   NULL,   NULL,                  '+1555010200', '60601', 'patel'),
        (10, 'web',   NULL,   NULL,                  NULL,          '94105', 'rivera')
)
SELECT *
FROM customer_stage
ORDER BY row_id;

sections.heading: Write the duplicate rule before the query
paragraphs: A useful duplicate rule has three parts: the scope of the identifier, the fallback evidence, and the decision outcome. Without all three, the implementation will usually smuggle in assumptions that are hard to review later.

For the hypothetical fixture, the duplicate policy can be written as follows. First, if source_system and external_customer_id are both present and equal, the rows identify the same source customer. Second, if a row is missing external_customer_id, it may be linked to a known customer using fallback evidence, but only when that fallback evidence maps to exactly one known source customer. Third, if fallback evidence maps to multiple known source customers, the result is ambiguous and should not be merged automatically. Fourth, if all compared rows are missing external_customer_id, matching fallback evidence can create a provisional duplicate group, not a permanent identifier.

The word provisional matters. Fallback evidence is not the same kind of fact as an issued identifier. An email address can be shared. A phone can be reassigned. A postal code is not person-specific. A last name can change. The model may still choose to use those attributes, but it should preserve the difference between an identifier and evidence.

Also note the source scope. Row 7 has external_customer_id C100 from store, while rows 1 and 2 have C100 from web. Unless the business has established that C100 is a global identifier across both systems, source_system plus external_customer_id is the key. The identical text C100 is not enough by itself.
bullets: Identifier rule: source_system plus external_customer_id is a duplicate key when external_customer_id is present.
Fallback rule: email plus last name, or phone plus postal code plus last name when email is missing, can produce candidate evidence.
Ambiguity rule: fallback evidence that points to multiple known identifiers is not an automatic merge.
Insufficient evidence rule: rows with no usable identifier and no usable fallback key remain unresolved.

sections.heading: A diagnostic query for candidate pairs
paragraphs: The following diagnostic turns each row into one or more pieces of identity evidence, joins rows that share the same evidence, and classifies the pair. It is written as illustrative SQL using common relational operations such as common table expressions, unions, joins, grouping, and case expressions. It should be adapted and verified against the target database before publication or operational use.

The important modeling choice is that fallback evidence is not treated as equal to the external identifier. Instead, it is used to classify candidate pairs. Known identifier conflicts remain visible. Missing-identifier rows can be linked only when the fallback key has one known destination.

codeExamples.code:
WITH customer_stage (
    row_id,
    source_system,
    external_customer_id,
    email_norm,
    phone_e164,
    postal_code,
    last_name_norm
) AS (
    VALUES
        (1,  'web',   'C100', 'ada@example.test',    '+1555010100', '02139', 'lovelace'),
        (2,  'web',   'C100', 'ada.new@example.test','+1555010100', '02139', 'lovelace'),
        (3,  'web',   NULL,   'ada@example.test',    '+1555010100', '02139', 'lovelace'),
        (4,  'web',   'C200', 'shared@example.test', '+1555010101', '10001', 'chen'),
        (5,  'web',   'C201', 'shared@example.test', '+1555010101', '10001', 'chen'),
        (6,  'web',   NULL,   'shared@example.test', '+1555010101', '10001', 'chen'),
        (7,  'store', 'C100', 'ada@example.test',    '+1555010100', '02139', 'lovelace'),
        (8,  'web',   NULL,   NULL,                  '+1555010200', '60601', 'patel'),
        (9,  'web',   NULL,   NULL,                  '+1555010200', '60601', 'patel'),
        (10, 'web',   NULL,   NULL,                  NULL,          '94105', 'rivera')
),
identity_evidence AS (
    SELECT
        row_id,
        'external' AS evidence_type,
        source_system || ':' || external_customer_id AS evidence_value
    FROM customer_stage
    WHERE external_customer_id IS NOT NULL

    UNION ALL

    SELECT
        row_id,
        'email_last' AS evidence_type,
        email_norm || ':' || last_name_norm AS evidence_value
    FROM customer_stage
    WHERE email_norm IS NOT NULL
      AND last_name_norm IS NOT NULL

    UNION ALL

    SELECT
        row_id,
        'phone_postal_last' AS evidence_type,
        phone_e164 || ':' || postal_code || ':' || last_name_norm AS evidence_value
    FROM customer_stage
    WHERE email_norm IS NULL
      AND phone_e164 IS NOT NULL
      AND postal_code IS NOT NULL
      AND last_name_norm IS NOT NULL
),
known_destinations AS (
    SELECT
        e.evidence_type,
        e.evidence_value,
        COUNT(DISTINCT c.source_system || ':' || c.external_customer_id) AS known_identifier_count
    FROM identity_evidence e
    JOIN customer_stage c
      ON c.row_id = e.row_id
    WHERE e.evidence_type <> 'external'
      AND c.external_customer_id IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY e.evidence_type, e.evidence_value
),
candidate_pairs AS (
    SELECT
        e1.evidence_type,
        e1.evidence_value,
        e1.row_id AS left_row_id,
        e2.row_id AS right_row_id
    FROM identity_evidence e1
    JOIN identity_evidence e2
      ON e1.evidence_type = e2.evidence_type
     AND e1.evidence_value = e2.evidence_value
     AND e1.row_id < e2.row_id
)
SELECT
    p.evidence_type,
    p.evidence_value,
    p.left_row_id,
    p.right_row_id,
    CASE
        WHEN p.evidence_type = 'external' THEN
            'duplicate: same source-scoped external identifier'
        WHEN l.external_customer_id IS NOT NULL
         AND r.external_customer_id IS NOT NULL THEN
            'do not auto-merge: fallback collides across known identifiers'
        WHEN COALESCE(k.known_identifier_count, 0) > 1 THEN
            'unresolved: missing identifier matches multiple known identifiers'
        WHEN COALESCE(k.known_identifier_count, 0) = 1 THEN
            'provisional duplicate: missing identifier has one known destination'
        ELSE
            'provisional duplicate: only missing-identifier rows share fallback evidence'
    END AS duplicate_decision
FROM candidate_pairs p
JOIN customer_stage l
  ON l.row_id = p.left_row_id
JOIN customer_stage r
  ON r.row_id = p.right_row_id
LEFT JOIN known_destinations k
  ON k.evidence_type = p.evidence_type
 AND k.evidence_value = p.evidence_value
ORDER BY p.left_row_id, p.right_row_id, p.evidence_type;

sections.heading: What the diagnostic is protecting against
paragraphs: The first protection is against treating all NULL identifiers as one bucket. If the grouping key is just external_customer_id, every missing value is either excluded by database semantics or mishandled by application logic. Neither outcome expresses the business rule. Missing identifiers need a separate decision path.

The second protection is against over-merging through fallback attributes. Suppose a rule says that any shared email, phone, or postal code is enough to merge. In the fixture, rows 4 and 5 would collapse even though the source has issued two distinct customer identifiers. Row 6 would then be pulled into that merged group. That may be correct after human review or after a trusted crosswalk is introduced, but it is not justified by the nullable identifier alone.

The third protection is against non-transitive matching. Pairwise matching rules can form chains: row A matches row B by email, row B matches row C by phone, and row A does not match row C at all. If the pipeline converts that chain into a single customer without a policy for precedence and conflicts, the duplicate group is an artifact of the algorithm rather than a stated business rule.

The fourth protection is against losing unresolved rows. Row 10 is not clean or dirty; it is undecidable under the current rule. That is a valid modeling outcome. A good duplicate policy should make room for known, duplicate, ambiguous, and unresolved states.

sections.heading: Turning the rule into a modeling contract
paragraphs: The durable artifact is not the SQL itself. It is the modeling contract that the SQL expresses. For nullable business identifiers, the contract should say which attributes can identify an entity, which attributes are merely evidence, how conflicts are handled, and what status is assigned when the data is insufficient.

A compact contract for the hypothetical example could be: source_system plus external_customer_id is the source-scoped customer identifier when present; fallback evidence may suggest a duplicate for rows with missing identifiers; fallback evidence cannot override conflicting known identifiers; and unresolved rows remain loadable but are not assigned to a canonical customer without more evidence.

This contract also separates identity from measurement. If a warehouse later records durations, lags, or lifecycle facts, those facts should hang off a stable modeled entity or an explicitly provisional one. They should not depend on an accidental grouping of NULL identifiers. That is the connection to dimensional modeling practice: first define the grain and identity of the thing being measured, then attach facts to it.

The tradeoff is conservative matching. Some true duplicates will remain unresolved until more evidence arrives. That is usually preferable to silent over-merge when identifiers are missing, because over-merge corrupts history in a way that can be difficult to unwind. If the business wants aggressive matching, the model can support it, but the rule should name the risk and preserve the evidence that caused the merge.
bullets: Keep the issued identifier, fallback evidence, and final duplicate decision as separate concepts.
Record ambiguity as a first-class outcome instead of forcing every row into a duplicate or non-duplicate bucket.
Use fallback rules that are explainable to the people who own the source data.

takeaways: Two NULL business identifiers are not evidence that two rows identify the same entity.
When an external identifier is missing, define fallback evidence and ambiguity handling explicitly instead of relying on a generic equality rule.
Fallback attributes can support provisional duplicate decisions, but they should not silently override conflicting known identifiers.
A practical duplicate rule should produce at least four outcomes: duplicate, provisional duplicate, ambiguous, and unresolved.

title: Domain constraints for categorical data
description: A practical guide to choosing controlled vocabularies for categorical data while keeping unknown, not applicable, and invalid values separate.
lead: Controlled vocabularies make categorical data usable, but they often fail in a subtle way: they mix legitimate business values with missing, inapplicable, and invalid inputs. The result is a column that looks constrained while still answering the wrong question.

sections.heading: The modeling problem
paragraphs: A domain constraint says what values are allowed for an attribute. For categorical data, that usually means a controlled vocabulary such as web, store, phone, and marketplace for an order channel. The hard part is not writing the constraint. The hard part is deciding what belongs in the domain.

Practitioners often reach for a convenient extra value such as unknown, none, other, or n/a. Sometimes that is correct. Often it is a modeling shortcut that collapses several different states into one bucket. A value can be unknown because the source did not send it. It can be invalid because the source sent a value outside the agreed vocabulary. It can be not applicable because the attribute does not make sense for that row. Those states need different handling.

This article uses a hypothetical retail order example. The goal is to choose a controlled vocabulary for a categorical attribute without confusing unknown and invalid values. It assumes you are already comfortable with candidate keys and alternate keys, because the examples use stable codes as keys for reference data.

sections.heading: Counterexample: one column that tries to do everything
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical order feed with one categorical field named order_channel. The business wants to classify orders by the channel where the order was placed. A first pass might define a column with these allowed values: web, store, phone, marketplace, unknown, and other.

That design feels tidy because every row can have a non-null value. It is also ambiguous. Unknown might mean the source sent no value, the integration failed, a historical file lacked the field, or the order was imported before the channel taxonomy existed. Other might mean a real channel outside the vocabulary, a typo, or a new partner that should be added to the vocabulary. Once these cases are loaded as ordinary categories, downstream users cannot tell whether they are looking at customer behavior or data quality.

Use this hypothetical raw input as the fixture: event 1001 has raw channel WEB, event 1002 has raw channel Store, event 1003 has no raw channel, event 1004 has raw channel TikTok Live, event 1005 has raw channel web, and event 1006 has raw channel KIOSK-7. By inspection, WEB, Store, and web can be normalized into known values if the vocabulary allows web and store. The missing value for 1003 is unknown. TikTok Live and KIOSK-7 are not unknown; they are observed inputs that are not currently valid order_channel codes.

The counterexample is to map 1003 to unknown and both 1004 and 1006 to other. That preserves row counts but destroys meaning. Missing input and unexpected input become indistinguishable from a deliberate business bucket. If TikTok Live later becomes an approved channel, you cannot reliably find the historical rows that should be reclassified unless you retained the raw value and its resolution status.

codeExamples.code:
-- Counterexample: this looks constrained, but it mixes business values with data-quality states.
CREATE TABLE bad_order_event (
  order_event_id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  order_channel text NOT NULL,
  CHECK (order_channel IN ('web', 'store', 'phone', 'marketplace', 'unknown', 'other'))
);

-- These rows are all accepted, but the model cannot explain why they are unknown or other.
INSERT INTO bad_order_event (order_event_id, order_channel) VALUES
  (1001, 'web'),
  (1002, 'store'),
  (1003, 'unknown'),
  (1004, 'other'),
  (1005, 'web'),
  (1006, 'other');

sections.heading: Separate the vocabulary from the resolution
paragraphs: A better design separates the controlled vocabulary from the resolution of incoming data. The vocabulary contains valid business categories. The resolution records what happened when raw input was interpreted. That gives you two different questions with two different answers: what valid category does this row have, and how confidently was that category derived?

For the hypothetical order_channel attribute, the business vocabulary might contain only web, store, phone, and marketplace. It should not contain unknown just because an upstream system sometimes omits the field. It should not contain other just because new raw values may appear. If a new channel is real and approved, add it deliberately to the vocabulary. If it is not approved, keep it out and treat the incoming row as an exception or unresolved observation.

The following illustrative SQL uses a reference table for the vocabulary and a separate resolution column on the event. The exact syntax may need adjustment for a specific database, but the relational shape is the important part: valid codes are referenced by key, missing and invalid observations do not become fake codes, and raw input is retained for diagnosis.

codeExamples.code:
CREATE TABLE order_channel (
  channel_code text PRIMARY KEY,
  display_name text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  is_active boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  CHECK (channel_code = lower(channel_code)),
  CHECK (channel_code <> '')
);

INSERT INTO order_channel (channel_code, display_name) VALUES
  ('web', 'Web'),
  ('store', 'Store'),
  ('phone', 'Phone'),
  ('marketplace', 'Marketplace');

CREATE TABLE order_event (
  order_event_id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  raw_channel_text text,
  channel_code text REFERENCES order_channel (channel_code),
  channel_resolution text NOT NULL,
  CHECK (channel_resolution IN ('matched', 'missing', 'invalid')),
  CHECK (
    (channel_resolution = 'matched' AND channel_code IS NOT NULL)
    OR
    (channel_resolution IN ('missing', 'invalid') AND channel_code IS NULL)
  )
);

INSERT INTO order_event
  (order_event_id, raw_channel_text, channel_code, channel_resolution)
VALUES
  (1001, 'WEB', 'web', 'matched'),
  (1002, 'Store', 'store', 'matched'),
  (1003, NULL, NULL, 'missing'),
  (1004, 'TikTok Live', NULL, 'invalid'),
  (1005, 'web', 'web', 'matched'),
  (1006, 'KIOSK-7', NULL, 'invalid');

sections.heading: Decision tests for special values
paragraphs: The main design decision is whether a special label belongs in the business domain or in data-quality metadata. These tests are useful before adding values such as unknown, other, none, or not_applicable to a controlled vocabulary.

First, ask whether the value describes the real-world entity or only your knowledge of it. If a later file can replace unknown with web without the underlying order changing, unknown was not a business category. It was a statement about missing knowledge. Store that as null plus a resolution reason, or as a separate status column, not as a member of the order_channel vocabulary.

Second, ask whether the value is known to be inapplicable. Not applicable is different from unknown. Suppose a hypothetical product table has delivery_method with values physical_ship, pickup, and digital_delivery. For a purely informational subscription that never has delivery, not_applicable may be a true business state if the business explicitly defines it that way. But if the source simply failed to provide delivery_method, using not_applicable would be wrong. The test is whether you know the attribute does not apply, not whether you lack a value.

Third, ask whether other is stable enough to analyze. Other can be a valid business category when the business intentionally offers an option named Other and does not need more detail. It is not a safe dumping ground for malformed, new, or unmapped source values. If raw values are meaningful enough to triage later, keep them in an exception table or raw column.

Fourth, ask who owns the vocabulary. If multiple fact tables, marts, or products use the same category, a shared reference table is usually safer than repeated check constraints. Kimball’s conformed dimension guidance is relevant here: shared dimensions help preserve consistent interpretation across processes. A small check constraint can be fine for a private, stable, local status, but it is less suitable for a vocabulary that needs stewardship, display names, deprecation, or cross-model reuse.
bullets: If the value means the source did not tell us, model it as missing knowledge.
If the value means the source told us something outside the contract, model it as invalid input.
If the value means the attribute truly does not apply, define that explicitly and keep it separate from missing.
If the value is a real business option, it can belong in the controlled vocabulary.
If the value is a temporary load accommodation, do not let it masquerade as a business category.

sections.heading: Diagnostics that preserve meaning
paragraphs: Once the vocabulary and resolution are separate, diagnostics become straightforward. You can report business distribution using only matched rows, and you can report data-quality problems using the resolution fields. The important point is that no query has to infer whether other means missing, malformed, or newly discovered.

For the hypothetical six-row fixture above, the business distribution by valid channel is web equals 2 and store equals 1. Missing is 1. Invalid is 2. Those numbers are different facts. Combining them into channel counts would overstate business categories and hide onboarding work for new values.

A useful diagnostic query should show the unresolved raw values, not just their count. If KIOSK-7 appears once, it may be a typo, test data, or a store device code. If it appears ten thousand times, the vocabulary may need a new channel or a mapping rule. Either way, the decision should be made from retained evidence, not from a pre-collapsed other bucket.

codeExamples.code:
-- Business distribution: only valid matched categories.
SELECT
  channel_code,
  count(*) AS order_events
FROM order_event
WHERE channel_resolution = 'matched'
GROUP BY channel_code
ORDER BY channel_code;

-- Data-quality distribution: missing and invalid are visible as separate states.
SELECT
  channel_resolution,
  count(*) AS order_events
FROM order_event
GROUP BY channel_resolution
ORDER BY channel_resolution;

-- Triage invalid observed inputs without promoting them into the vocabulary.
SELECT
  raw_channel_text,
  count(*) AS occurrences
FROM order_event
WHERE channel_resolution = 'invalid'
GROUP BY raw_channel_text
ORDER BY occurrences DESC, raw_channel_text;

sections.heading: Constraint choices and tradeoffs
paragraphs: There are several legitimate implementation choices. A check constraint is compact and close to the table. It works well for tiny, stable sets whose meaning is local to one table. Examples might include a processing state such as pending, processed, and failed. The tradeoff is that changing the set usually means changing table definition, and it provides little room for names, descriptions, ownership, or lifecycle metadata.

A reference table is better when the vocabulary is shared, governed, or likely to evolve. It lets you attach display names, sort order, active flags, effective dates, or stewardship notes without changing every dependent table. A foreign key prevents invalid codes from entering modeled data while still allowing null when the relationship is optional. If the relationship is required, combine the foreign key with a not-null constraint; the foreign key alone does not mean every row must have a category.

Dimensional models sometimes use an unknown dimension row so a fact table can keep a non-null surrogate key even when descriptive context arrives late. Kimball’s late-arriving dimension pattern is useful background for that case. The key distinction is that an unknown dimension row is a warehouse loading and query convention, not proof that unknown is a natural business value. Keep the natural category, raw input, and resolution semantics clear even if a downstream dimensional table uses a surrogate unknown member for referential completeness.

The practical rule is simple: constrain valid business values tightly, but do not force every observation to pretend it has one. Unknown, invalid, and not applicable are not interchangeable. Model the difference before it reaches reporting, because dashboards rarely have enough context to recover it later.

takeaways: A controlled vocabulary should contain valid business categories, not every state your pipeline may encounter while trying to classify a row.
Unknown means the value is not known; invalid means a value was observed but is outside the allowed domain. They require different storage, diagnostics, and remediation.
Keep raw input and resolution status when classifying source values. This preserves the ability to add mappings, fix source contracts, and explain historical counts.

Use check constraints for small local vocabularies and reference tables for shared or governed vocabularies. Pair nullable foreign keys with explicit resolution fields when missing values are allowed.
An unknown dimension member can be useful in dimensional modeling, but it should not be confused with a natural business category in the controlled vocabulary.

title: Relational division for analytical questions
description: A practical guide to finding entities that satisfy every requirement in a reference set, using a small hypothetical retail dataset with counterexamples and two SQL patterns.
lead: Many analytical questions are not asking whether an entity matches one condition. They ask whether it matches every condition in a reference set: every required product, every onboarding step, every permission, every checklist item, or every expected event. That pattern is relational division. This article shows how to recognize it, model the supporting relations, and query it without accidentally accepting entities that only satisfy some requirements.

sections.heading: The shape of the question
paragraphs: Relational division answers questions of the form: find each entity X such that, for every required value Y in a reference set, the pair X-Y exists in an observed relation. In analytical work, X might be a customer, account, store, device, campaign, or user. Y might be a required product, consent, onboarding step, country, entitlement, or milestone.

The key phrase is every requirement. If the question says any, at least one, top N, latest, first, or most, it is probably not relational division. If the question says all, every, complete, fully eligible, has the full bundle, passed the full checklist, or contains each item in the standard set, relational division is likely the right mental model.

A common mistake is to start from the observed facts and count how many rows each entity has. That can work only if the reference set is explicit, the fact table has the right grain, and duplicates are controlled. Relational division is safer when you name the divisor: the table or query that represents the required set. Then you ask which entities are not missing any row from that set.
bullets: Dividend: the observed relation, such as customer-product purchases.
Divisor: the required reference set, such as products in the starter bundle.
Quotient: the entities that satisfy every requirement, such as customers who bought every starter-bundle product.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail fixture with counterexamples
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail dataset. The business question is: which customers bought every product in the required starter bundle? The reference set contains three products: coffee beans, filters, and grinder. A customer qualifies only if the customer has purchased all three required products at least once.

The important modeling point is that the fact relation should be considered at the customer-product grain for this question. If a customer bought filters twice, that duplicate purchase should not count as two different required products. If a customer bought a non-required product, that extra product should not help. If a customer bought only two of the three products, they should not qualify.

The following fixture includes deliberate counterexamples. Customer 101 qualifies. Customer 102 is missing grinder. Customer 103 bought an extra mug but is missing filters. Customer 104 qualifies even though coffee beans appear twice. Customer 105 bought only non-required products and should not qualify.

codeExamples.code:
WITH
required_products(product_id, product_name) AS (
  VALUES
    (10, 'coffee beans'),
    (20, 'filters'),
    (30, 'grinder')
),
customer_purchases(customer_id, product_id) AS (
  VALUES
    (101, 10), (101, 20), (101, 30),
    (102, 10), (102, 20),
    (103, 10), (103, 30), (103, 40),
    (104, 10), (104, 10), (104, 20), (104, 30),
    (105, 40), (105, 50)
)
SELECT *
FROM required_products;

-- Expected qualifying customers for the stated question: 101 and 104.

sections.heading: The NOT EXISTS pattern: no missing requirements
paragraphs: The most direct SQL expression of relational division is a double negative: return customers for whom there does not exist a required product that the customer has not purchased. This sounds awkward in English, but it maps cleanly to the logic of the question.

The outer query chooses candidate entities. The first NOT EXISTS says: do not allow a missing requirement to exist. The inner NOT EXISTS checks whether the current customer has a purchase row for the current required product. If the inner check fails for any required product, the customer is rejected.

This pattern is valuable because it preserves the meaning of every requirement. It does not depend on the number of purchases a customer made. It does not give credit for non-required products. It handles duplicate fact rows because the inner existence check only asks whether at least one matching row exists.

codeExamples.code:
WITH
required_products(product_id, product_name) AS (
  VALUES
    (10, 'coffee beans'),
    (20, 'filters'),
    (30, 'grinder')
),
customer_purchases(customer_id, product_id) AS (
  VALUES
    (101, 10), (101, 20), (101, 30),
    (102, 10), (102, 20),
    (103, 10), (103, 30), (103, 40),
    (104, 10), (104, 10), (104, 20), (104, 30),
    (105, 40), (105, 50)
),
candidate_customers AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id
  FROM customer_purchases
)
SELECT c.customer_id
FROM candidate_customers AS c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM required_products AS r
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM customer_purchases AS p
    WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND p.product_id = r.product_id
  )
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

-- Expected result:
-- 101
-- 104

sections.heading: The counting pattern and its boundaries
paragraphs: A second common implementation joins purchases to the required set, groups by customer, and compares the number of distinct required products purchased with the size of the reference set. This is compact and often easier for analysts to read. It is correct when the required set has one row per required value and the observed relation is counted at the same logical grain.

The distinct count matters. Without it, customer 104 would have four matching purchase rows because coffee beans appear twice. A plain COUNT(*) would compare 4 to 3 and incorrectly reject a qualifying customer. Conversely, an entity with duplicates for one required product but missing another might be incorrectly accepted if the query only counts rows and does not count distinct required values.

The denominator also matters. It must come from the reference set, not from the customer’s observed products. If the query asks whether each customer bought three different products, it is no longer answering whether they bought the three required products. Customer 103 bought three distinct products in the fixture, but one is a mug and filters are missing. Counting any three products would produce a false positive.

codeExamples.code:
WITH
required_products(product_id, product_name) AS (
  VALUES
    (10, 'coffee beans'),
    (20, 'filters'),
    (30, 'grinder')
),
customer_purchases(customer_id, product_id) AS (
  VALUES
    (101, 10), (101, 20), (101, 30),
    (102, 10), (102, 20),
    (103, 10), (103, 30), (103, 40),
    (104, 10), (104, 10), (104, 20), (104, 30),
    (105, 40), (105, 50)
),
required_count AS (
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM required_products
)
SELECT p.customer_id
FROM customer_purchases AS p
JOIN required_products AS r
  ON r.product_id = p.product_id
CROSS JOIN required_count AS rc
GROUP BY p.customer_id, rc.n
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id) = rc.n
ORDER BY p.customer_id;

-- Expected result:
-- 101
-- 104

sections.heading: Counterexamples to catch before trusting the result
paragraphs: Relational division queries can look plausible while answering the wrong question. The safest way to review them is to keep a few counterexamples in the fixture and confirm that each one behaves as expected. These counterexamples are not performance tests; they are semantic tests of the model and query.

First, include an entity that satisfies all but one requirement. This catches queries that use OR logic or that accidentally ask for any required product. In the hypothetical fixture, customer 102 bought coffee beans and filters but not grinder. They must be excluded.

Second, include an entity with extra non-required values. This catches queries that count total distinct values instead of required values. Customer 103 bought coffee beans, grinder, and a mug. Three distinct products are not enough, because the missing required product is filters.

Third, include duplicate observed rows. This catches queries that use COUNT(*) at the fact grain when the question is about distinct requirement satisfaction. Customer 104 bought coffee beans twice but still qualifies because duplicates should not harm the answer. A query that rejects customer 104 because there are four matching rows is using the wrong grain.

Fourth, decide what an empty reference set means. In formal relational division, every candidate entity satisfies every requirement in an empty set because there is no missing requirement. In business analytics, an empty required-products table often means the setup is broken, not that every customer qualifies. The correct behavior is a business rule, but it must be explicit. A guardrail query can fail the job or return no rows when the divisor is unexpectedly empty.

Fifth, check nullable identifiers. If product_id can be null in either relation, equality comparisons may not behave as a business user expects. For this kind of question, requirement identifiers should be non-null and stable. That is a modeling prerequisite, not a query trick.
bullets: All-but-one entity: should be excluded.
Extra-values entity: should be excluded unless all required values are also present.
Duplicate-facts entity: should still be handled at the required-value grain.
Empty divisor: should be defined deliberately before the query is used.
Null identifiers: should be prevented or handled before division logic is trusted.

codeExamples.code:
-- A compact diagnostic for missing required products by customer.
-- This is useful for reviewing false negatives and explaining exclusions.
WITH
required_products(product_id, product_name) AS (
  VALUES
    (10, 'coffee beans'),
    (20, 'filters'),
    (30, 'grinder')
),
customer_purchases(customer_id, product_id) AS (
  VALUES
    (101, 10), (101, 20), (101, 30),
    (102, 10), (102, 20),
    (103, 10), (103, 30), (103, 40),
    (104, 10), (104, 10), (104, 20), (104, 30),
    (105, 40), (105, 50)
),
candidate_customers AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id
  FROM customer_purchases
)
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  r.product_id AS missing_product_id,
  r.product_name AS missing_product_name
FROM candidate_customers AS c
CROSS JOIN required_products AS r
LEFT JOIN customer_purchases AS p
  ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id
 AND p.product_id = r.product_id
WHERE p.customer_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customer_id, r.product_id;

-- Expected diagnostic rows include:
-- 102 missing grinder
-- 103 missing filters
-- 105 missing coffee beans, filters, and grinder

sections.heading: Modeling prerequisites for reliable division
paragraphs: Relational division depends on clean relationship tables. Before writing the query, define the entity identifier, the requirement identifier, and the grain of the observed relation. For the hypothetical example, the relevant observed relation is not order lines as sold, with quantity, price, timestamp, and promotion details. It is the derived customer-product relationship: one customer has purchased one product at least once within the analysis scope.

Candidate keys matter because they state what makes a row unique. In the required set, product_id should identify one required product. In a persisted customer-product satisfaction table, customer_id plus product_id would commonly be the logical uniqueness rule. Even if the raw event table contains duplicates or repeated purchases, the relationship used for division should have a clear grain.

Do not hide the reference set inside ad hoc CASE expressions if it is a reusable business concept. A named table or view for the required set makes the divisor reviewable. It also lets the same reference set support a diagnostic query, a completeness metric, and the final qualifying-entities query.

This article intentionally stays at the relational semantics level. Engine-specific indexing, optimizer behavior, and execution plans are separate performance concerns. The immediate goal is to make sure the question, the reference set, and the observed relation all have the same meaning before anyone tries to make the query faster.

sections.heading: When to use which form
paragraphs: Use the NOT EXISTS form when correctness needs to be obvious from the logic of missing requirements. It is especially clear when the reference set is small, when you need to explain why an entity failed, or when you want the query to read like the business rule: no required item is missing.

Use the counting form when the relationship grain is already well controlled and the team is comfortable with distinct counts over the required identifier. It can be concise for dashboard models and eligibility flags, but it should be paired with counterexamples that prove duplicates and extra values do not change the answer.

A practical workflow is to start with the missing-requirements diagnostic, then write the NOT EXISTS division query, then optionally translate to the counting form if it is easier to maintain in the target modeling layer. If the two forms disagree on the same fixture, the issue is usually a grain problem, a duplicate problem, a nullable key, or a reference-set mismatch.

takeaways: Relational division answers every requirement questions: find entities for which no required reference value is missing.
Keep the divisor explicit. The reference set should be a named table, view, or query with one row per required value.
Use counterexamples to validate semantics: all-but-one, extra values, duplicate facts, empty reference set, and null identifiers.
The NOT EXISTS form expresses relational division directly; the counting form is acceptable only when it counts distinct required values at the correct grain.
Modeling clarity comes before performance tuning: define the entity key, requirement key, and observed relationship grain before optimizing the SQL.

title: Temporal uniqueness constraints
description: A practical guide to deciding when two records are allowed to share the same identifier across time, using a hypothetical customer badge dataset and overlap diagnostics.
lead: A normal uniqueness rule answers one question: can two rows have the same value now? Temporal uniqueness constraints answer a harder question: can two rows share an identifier if their facts are true during different periods? The difference matters whenever identifiers are reassigned, corrected, versioned, or loaded from systems that preserve history.

sections.heading: The question temporal uniqueness answers
paragraphs: A candidate key says that a set of attributes uniquely identifies a tuple in a relation. In a simple customer table, customer_id might be unique because no two current customer rows should use the same identifier. Temporal data changes the meaning of that statement. Once a table records valid_from and valid_to, the same identifier may appear more than once, but not necessarily at the same time.

A temporal uniqueness constraint defines the conditions under which two records are allowed to share an identifier across time. It is not just a physical database index. It is a business rule over identifiers, scopes, and validity periods.

The core decision can be stated plainly: for identifier X, are two distinct records allowed to be true for overlapping periods? If no, then the identifier is temporally unique within the chosen scope. If yes, then the identifier is not the thing being constrained, or the constraint is missing another attribute such as store_id, issuing_system, tenant_id, or relationship_type.

This article uses a hypothetical customer badge assignment dataset. The same reasoning applies to account ownership, subscription plans, product codes, territory assignments, employee roles, and slowly changing dimensions. The point is not the retail example; the point is learning to say exactly when sharing an identifier is valid.

sections.heading: A hypothetical badge assignment table
paragraphs: Assume a retailer issues loyalty badges. A physical badge_id can be assigned to one customer at a time. A badge can later be returned, retired, or reassigned. The table records business validity, not load time. Dates use half-open intervals: valid_from is included, valid_to is excluded. Under that convention, a row ending on 2026-04-01 and another row starting on 2026-04-01 do not overlap.

Here is the intended relation: BadgeAssignment(record_id, badge_id, customer_id, valid_from, valid_to). A null valid_to means the assignment is still current. For reasoning and diagnostics, null can be treated as an open-ended future value, as long as that convention is explicit.

The business rule is: within the retailer, one badge_id may belong to at most one customer at any instant of business time. The same badge_id may appear in multiple rows only when the periods do not overlap. That rule is narrower than saying badge_id is globally unique forever, and stronger than saying each row merely needs a distinct record_id.
bullets: record_id is the row identifier. It distinguishes historical records from one another.
badge_id is the reusable business identifier being constrained over time.
customer_id is the entity receiving the badge.
valid_from and valid_to define when the assignment is true in business time.
The temporal uniqueness rule applies to badge_id and the validity period, not to record_id.

sections.heading: Work through the counterexamples
paragraphs: Rows 1 and 2 share badge_id R-100. That is allowed under the half-open rule because row 1 is valid from 2026-01-01 up to, but not including, 2026-04-01. Row 2 starts on 2026-04-01. There is no instant at which both rows are true. This is the standard case where two historical records can share an identifier across time.

Rows 2 and 3 also share badge_id R-100, but they overlap. Row 2 is valid from 2026-04-01 to 2026-07-01. Row 3 is valid from 2026-06-15 to 2026-08-01. From 2026-06-15 through the instant before 2026-07-01, the same badge appears assigned to two customer records. If the business rule says one badge can belong to only one customer at a time, row 3 violates temporal uniqueness.

Rows 4 and 5 show the common null-current problem. If valid_to is null for row 4, and null means open-ended, then row 4 overlaps every later row for badge_id R-200 unless row 4 is first closed. Row 5 is therefore invalid because it assigns R-200 to C-55 during a period when R-200 is still assigned to C-42.

Row 6 is a different kind of bad record. With half-open intervals, [2026-03-01, 2026-03-01) is empty. It does not assign the badge at any instant. Empty intervals should usually be rejected with a period-validity rule such as valid_from < valid_to, separate from the temporal uniqueness rule.

Rows 7 and 8 are valid if valid_to is exclusive. They would be ambiguous or invalid under an inclusive-end model because both would include 2026-06-01. This is why a temporal uniqueness rule must define boundary semantics before anyone writes constraints, merge logic, or dashboard filters.

sections.heading: Write the rule before the constraint
paragraphs: A useful temporal uniqueness constraint has four parts: the identifier, the scope, the period, and the overlap rule. Leaving any part implicit creates room for contradictory data that still looks reasonable row by row.

For the badge example, the identifier is badge_id. The scope is the retailer as a whole. If the same badge numbers can be issued independently by different stores, then store_id belongs in the scope and two stores may both have badge R-100 without conflict. If badge numbers are globally issued, store_id must not be added just to make conflicts disappear.

The period is business validity: when the badge assignment is true in the retailer’s operating model. That is different from system time, which records when the warehouse learned or stored the fact. Temporal uniqueness normally needs one chosen time basis. Mixing local store dates, UTC timestamps, and load timestamps in one rule produces false overlaps and false gaps. Multi-time-zone models should explicitly decide which time representation is used for comparisons.

The overlap rule in this article is half-open interval overlap. Two periods overlap when the first starts before the second ends and the second starts before the first ends. Using an artificial far-future value for open-ended rows, the predicate is: a.valid_from < b.valid_to and b.valid_from < a.valid_to. Two records can share the identifier only when that predicate is false.

This is the relational statement behind the rule: for any two distinct badge assignment records in the same scope, if their badge_id values are equal, then their validity periods must not overlap. Equivalently, if two distinct records have the same badge_id and overlapping validity periods, at least one of the records is wrong, incomplete, or in the wrong relation.
bullets: Identifier: which value is being reused or protected?
Scope: where must the identifier be unique, such as tenant, issuer, store, or source system?
Period: which time axis defines truth, such as business validity rather than load time?
Boundary rule: are intervals half-open, closed, date-grain, or timestamp-grain?
Exception policy: are corrections represented by replacing a row, closing a row, or adding a superseding row?

sections.heading: Diagnose overlaps with a query
paragraphs: A temporal uniqueness diagnostic looks for pairs of distinct rows with the same constrained identifier and overlapping periods. The following SQL is illustrative. It uses a far-future date to normalize null valid_to values for comparison. Before using this pattern in a production database, adapt the date literal, null convention, indexes, and constraint mechanism to the target engine.

This diagnostic should return pairs (2, 3) and (4, 5) for the hypothetical dataset. It should not return (1, 2) or (7, 8) because adjacent half-open intervals are allowed. A separate validity check should flag row 6 because its start is not before its end.

The query is not a substitute for a constraint. It is a way to inspect existing data, prove the rule to stakeholders, and build test fixtures. Once the intended rule is settled, the same semantics should be enforced as close to the write path as practical, using the constraint features available in the database or the ingestion system.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative temporal-overlap diagnostic for a badge assignment relation.
-- Assumes half-open periods: [valid_from, valid_to).
-- Assumes NULL valid_to means open-ended.

WITH normalized AS (
  SELECT
    record_id,
    badge_id,
    customer_id,
    valid_from,
    COALESCE(valid_to, DATE '9999-12-31') AS valid_to_for_check
  FROM badge_assignment
), overlap_pairs AS (
  SELECT
    a.record_id AS first_record_id,
    b.record_id AS second_record_id,
    a.badge_id,
    a.customer_id AS first_customer_id,
    b.customer_id AS second_customer_id,
    a.valid_from AS first_valid_from,
    a.valid_to_for_check AS first_valid_to,
    b.valid_from AS second_valid_from,
    b.valid_to_for_check AS second_valid_to
  FROM normalized a
  JOIN normalized b
    ON a.badge_id = b.badge_id
   AND a.record_id < b.record_id
   AND a.valid_from < b.valid_to_for_check
   AND b.valid_from < a.valid_to_for_check
)
SELECT *
FROM overlap_pairs
ORDER BY badge_id, first_record_id, second_record_id;

-- Separate period-validity diagnostic.
SELECT record_id, badge_id, customer_id, valid_from, valid_to
FROM badge_assignment
WHERE valid_to IS NOT NULL
  AND valid_from >= valid_to;

sections.heading: Common modeling mistakes
paragraphs: The first mistake is using a simple unique constraint on badge_id when reuse is allowed. That prevents valid historical reuse and forces people to invent new identifiers for the same real-world badge. If the identifier is reusable, plain uniqueness is too strong.

The second mistake is making the key too wide. A uniqueness rule on (badge_id, customer_id, valid_from) may prevent exact duplicate rows, but it does not prevent badge R-100 from being assigned to C-17 and C-42 at the same time. Adding attributes to a key can hide the violation if those attributes are not part of the business definition of uniqueness.

The third mistake is confusing row identity with business identity. record_id is useful because each row needs an addressable identity. It does not prove that the business facts are mutually consistent. A table can have perfectly unique record_id values and still claim that one badge belonged to two customers during the same week.

The fourth mistake is failing to define time grain and time zone. Date-grain periods can be enough for policies that change at midnight in a chosen business calendar. Timestamp-grain periods may be needed when changes happen during the day. In either case, comparisons need a consistent representation. Time-zone handling is a modeling decision, not an afterthought.

The fifth mistake is treating current-state rules and historical rules as the same thing. A current customer table might require badge_id to be unique among active rows. A history table needs the stronger temporal statement: uniqueness among records whose valid periods overlap.

sections.heading: Decision checklist
paragraphs: Use this checklist before implementing a temporal uniqueness constraint. It turns the vague question, can this identifier repeat, into a precise rule that can be reviewed, tested, and enforced.

If the answer to any item is unclear, do not start by choosing an index. Start by clarifying the relation. The constraint should reflect the intended meaning of the data, not merely the easiest structure to implement in one engine.
bullets: Name the identifier being constrained. Example: badge_id, product_code, account_number, subscription_id.
State whether the identifier is never reusable, reusable after a non-overlap, or allowed to overlap within a defined scope.
Define the scope. Example: global, tenant, issuing system, store, country, or source application.
Choose the time axis. Example: business validity, contractual validity, effective dating, or system recording time.
Choose interval boundaries. Half-open intervals usually make adjacency easier to reason about than inclusive-end intervals.
Define how open-ended rows are represented and compared.
Reject invalid periods before checking uniqueness.
Create counterexample rows that should fail and adjacent rows that should pass.
Keep row identity separate from the temporal business identifier.

takeaways: Two records can share a temporal identifier only when the business rule allows reuse and their validity periods do not overlap within the chosen scope.
Temporal uniqueness requires explicit interval semantics. Adjacent periods are valid under half-open intervals, while overlapping periods are not.
A unique row id or a wide duplicate-prevention key does not enforce temporal uniqueness. The rule must compare the constrained identifier across periods.
